articles.title: Qualcomm Dragonwing Nabs a Big SpaceX Starlink Mobile Nationwide US 5G Network Win
articles.summary: Qualcomm Dragonwing just landed a new US customer as part of the SpaceX Starlink mobile nationwide build-out The post Qualcomm Dragonwing Nabs a Big SpaceX Starlink Mobile Nationwide US 5G Network Win appeared first on ServeTheHome .
bodyEvidence: Qualcomm announced today that SpaceX has selected its Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure platforms to power Starlink Mobile’s U.S. nationwide terrestrial 5G network. The multi-year agreement covers tens of thousands of base station sites, with rollout planned to begin in 2027.

Starlink Mobile will deploy Massive MIMO radio units using 64 transmit and 64 receive paths (64T64R). That is a high-capacity antenna configuration designed to improve coverage, capacity, and spectral efficiency across the terrestrial network. The Dragonwing QRU100 platform provides highly integrated processing for these Massive MIMO radio units, supporting the radio functions behind that architecture. The Dragonwing QDU100 platform handles high-performance, efficient, latency-sensitive Layer 1 processing. It also sounds like Qualcomm is providing the L1 software for this deployment. That also means it sounds like the L2 and up are being handled by something else.

Qualcomm says the two platforms together are designed to improve performance per watt across both radio and distributed-unit processing. That energy efficiency improves network deployment economics when rolling out tens of thousands of sites. For a nationwide buildout, power draw at each location compounds quickly, and many tower sites face significant power constraints.

This is a significant win for Qualcomm’s Dragonwing infrastructure portfolio, which has been deployed in places like Asia but, from what we gather, has not been as popular in the US. It sounds like SpaceX plans to roll out the terrestrial network alongside its satellite constellation, giving Starlink Mobile a path to become a 4th major carrier in the US. The 2027 rollout start under a multi-year agreement means tens of thousands of sites will take time to deploy nationwide. Maybe the most interesting part will be whether SpaceX can accelerate deployment of its 5G network, as it has with its AI compute build-out.

rssBodyEvidence: AMD Q3 2026 earnings were massive with the data center and embedded segments seeing big uplift with the clear Venice x86 leadership looming
articles.title: AMD Q3 2026 Earnings Data Center Growth Drives Record Quarter
articles.summary: AMD Q3 2026 earnings were massive with the data center and embedded segments seeing big uplift with the clear Venice x86 leadership looming The post AMD Q3 2026 Earnings Data Center Growth Drives Record Quarter appeared first on ServeTheHome .
bodyEvidence: AMD posted a massive Q3 2026. Revenue hit $13.377 billion, up 45% year over year and 16% sequentially. Data Center revenue reached $8.546 billion, up 97% year over year. Embedded Revenue was up big, and client revenue fared better than Intel in many respects.
Here is AMD’s Q3 2026 summary slide. This is an enormous quarter. Embedded revenue was up 29% year over year, and yet that almost feels like a footnote.

AMD delivered GAAP operating income of $2.832 billion on revenue of $13.377 billion, with net income of $2.428 billion and diluted earnings per share of $1.46. On a non-GAAP basis, which excludes stock-based compensation, amortization of acquisition-related intangibles and other items, operating income was $3.923 billion, net income was $3.471 billion and EPS came in at $2.09.
Even the quarterly numbers were up a lot, with 16% growth on the GAAP side.

The Data Center segment generated $8.546 billion in revenue, up 97% year over year and 27% sequentially. AMD attributes this Data Center surge to strong EPYC demand and the launch of Instinct MI450 GPUs. The company says major clients, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, are running workloads on Helios rack-scale solutions powered by these chips.

The comparison to Intel’s data center results from last week saw its quarterly revenue of $7.3 billion, up 78% year-over-year. AMD’s Data Center segment at $8.546 billion grew faster at 97%. Both companies are clearly seeing surging demand for AI infrastructure and server processors, but AMD seems to be accelerating.

Venice is coming, and we expect AMD to have clear x86 performance leadership, as Intel’s PCIe Gen6 Diamond Rapids platform , we expect, will be later in 2027. On technical merits, we expect AMD to be in a great place, and it seems like AMD is better managing its supply to get chips out.
The combined Client and Gaming segment saw revenue down 8% year-over-year, at $3.722 billion. Client notched up a bit, while gaming went down. Memory and NAND prices are keeping a lid on this market.

Of note, AMD said its Ryzen AI Halo Platform with the Ryzen AI Max Pro 400 series is not available, so that means Gorgon Halo? We will have our first Gorgon Halo review soon, as that machine is running benchmarks now. Somewhat notable on the slide is that AMD has three AI-related products highlighted, while Intel’s three summary bullets on its CCPG segment were focused on shortages, demand for future products, and a generic AI PC nod. AMD, with the Strix Halo platform, at least has something it can use to run reasonably large models locally, and you have to wonder if that is a driver here.
The Embedded segment delivered $1.109 billion in revenue, up 29% year-over-year. AMD says growth came from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications and industrial end markets.

Just as a frame of reference, Xilinx’s annual revenue was something like $3.1-3.2B when AMD completed its acquisition of Xilinx . In most markets, if you grow 29% year over year and see a huge margin increase, it is time to throw a party. This seems to simply offset client’s (gaming) weakness.
AMD expects fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of approximately $17 billion plus or minus 3%. At the midpoint, that represents year-over-year growth of about 66% and sequential growth of roughly 27%.
If this quarter seems big, then next quarter seems like it will be significantly bigger.

AMD has its Helios rack-scale infrastructure rolling out, and Venice. Ryan recently went into the Venice architecture . If AMD was ahead in many metrics with its Turin generation , then adding more cores, updated cores, and higher memory bandwidth should be a recipe for clear x86 socket leadership, at least until Intel is able to field Diamond Rapids. It will be interesting to see how much of a price premium AMD can extract for a generational advantage and first-mover status. Socket refresh generations are less exciting than the Turin-to-Venice transition, which is a major platform update (DDR5 channel count and PCIe Gen6). That also means PCIe Gen6 development, like PCIe Gen4, will likely happen more often on AMD than on Intel. Gluing chips together seems to be working out reasonably well.

rssBodyEvidence: Marvell announced its intention to acquire Lumentum in a $115B acquisition to further optical connectivity in the AI era
articles.title: Marvell Proposes Acquiring Lumentum to Combine Optical Circuit Switching with AI Connectivity Silicon
articles.summary: Marvell announced its intention to acquire Lumentum in a $115B acquisition to further optical connectivity in the AI era The post Marvell Proposes Acquiring Lumentum to Combine Optical Circuit Switching with AI Connectivity Silicon appeared first on ServeTheHome .
bodyEvidence: Marvell Technology announced today that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Lumentum in an all-stock transaction with an implied value of about $115 billion. The proposed deal aims to merge Marvell’s electrical interconnect and custom silicon portfolio with Lumentum’s high-performance lasers, optical circuit switching (OCS), and compound semiconductor manufacturing capabilities. For AI infrastructure designers facing the physical limits of copper, this combination could drive deeper co-design across the entire signal chain, from distributed data centers to connections within advanced semiconductor packages.

The primary driver for this acquisition is the industry transition from electrical to optical connectivity as AI clusters scale. At the Marvell Computex 2026 Keynote , CEO Matt Murphy described connectivity as the next major bottleneck in data center design, noting that compute performance gains are outpacing connectivity and networking gains. Marvell has positioned itself to address this by offering solutions across various distances, from long-haul coherent links to short-reach scale-up domains. However, the “copper wall,” or the maximum distance copper can viably support before signal integrity fails, is moving closer as lane speeds increase. A copper-to-optics transition is underway in the industry, albeit slower than many people thought it would be 10 years ago.

Marvell’s existing portfolio addresses parts of this challenge with products like the COLORZ 800 module, which we examined in Going 800Gbps at up to 1000km with the Marvell COLORZ 800 . That module uses coherent detection and a local oscillator to maintain signal integrity over vast distances, packaging complex DSPs and photonics into a standard OSFP form factor. While effective for long-reach scale-across links, the move toward co-packaged optics (CPO) requires even tighter integration between the switch silicon and the optical engine.

The proposed combination pairs Marvell’s electrical and optical interconnect, CMOS/silicon photonics, switching/custom silicon design, and packaging expertise with Lumentum’s specialized compound semiconductor manufacturing, including indium phosphide (InP), plus high-speed and high-power lasers.

As we saw in our Marvell TX9190 CPO switch coverage from OCP 2025 , near-package optical engines shorten the electrical path, with fiber runs and pluggable light sources replacing long PCB traces. We also saw some neat technology on our recent AWS Networking Lab tour .
By acquiring Lumentum, Marvell intends to control more of this supply chain internally and design solutions across a larger domain instead of having to go to different companies for different parts.

Beyond component integration, Lumentum brings optical circuit switching (OCS) to the combined portfolio. The Lumentum R300 OCS establishes direct optical paths between endpoints using micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS) mirrors, eliminating intermediate packet processing and optical-electrical-optical (OEO) conversion along those switched paths. Lumentum says this results in dramatically lower latency, higher signal integrity, and significant reductions in network power for large GPU clusters.

Acquiring Lumentum and its technology will not come cheap, however. The $115 billion deal is being financed entirely with Marvell’s stock, significantly leveraging the value of the roughly $175 billion company in order to pay for the deal. In effect, this makes the deal closer to a merger than a buy-out. Following the settlement of the deal, Marvell shareholders will own 67% of the new company, while Lumentum shareholders will own the other 33%. Similarly, the deal will see three members of Lumentum’s board of directors join Marvell’s board, bringing it up to 10 members.

This deal, expected to close in the first half of 2028, so some time away, coordinates Marvell electrical and optical interconnect plus silicon design with Lumentum lasers, optical manufacturing, and OCS. The companies intend closer co-design and optimized, pre-validated optical solutions, faster time to market, and high-volume production, but that close is a long way away. This is a huge deal when companies are seeing valuations soar due to AI demand.

rssBodyEvidence: Qualcomm today is announcing that they have completed initial validation on their High Bandwidth Compute technology. The DRAM-stacked-upon-compute architecture moves on to commercialization, with Dragonfly AI250 set to sample in the first half of 2027
articles.title: Qualcomm Validates HBC Stacked Memory Ahead of 2027 Dragonfly AI250 Sampling
articles.summary: Qualcomm today is announcing that they have completed initial validation on their High Bandwidth Compute technology. The DRAM-stacked-upon-compute architecture moves on to commercialization, with Dragonfly AI250 set to sample in the first half of 2027 The post Qualcomm Validates HBC Stacked Memory Ahead of 2027 Dragonfly AI250 Sampling appeared first on ServeTheHome .
bodyEvidence: Qualcomm this morning is announcing that it has completed the initial validation of its High Bandwidth Compute (HBC) memory architecture, which will be a central part of the company’s upcoming Dragonfly data center AI accelerators. The stacked memory architecture will see Qualcomm and its manufacturing partners place multiple layers of DRAM on top of a small compute die in order to bring memory even closer to the compute hardware that is accessing it, allowing Qualcomm to reap the energy efficiency and cost efficiency benefits of a closer hardware placement.

The recent validation of the technology moves HBC one step closer to deployment in commercial products, which are scheduled to start sampling next year. Qualcomm has now validated that the technology works and is delivering energy efficiency and memory bandwidth close to their expectations, allowing them to move towards mass production next year while keeping customers (and investors) in the loop on the development of Qualcomm’s Dragonfly AI250 accelerator and its successors.

First announced by Qualcomm back at their 2026 Investor Day , HBC is a new Qualcomm-spearheaded technology that is intending to use near-memory compute in order to strike a new balance between memory capacity, memory performance, and production costs – with Qualcomm looking to push the envelope on all three aspects.

Fundamentally, the technology is a further variation on HBM and other memory stacking technologies. But unlike HBM where multiple DRAM dies are stacked on top of a base die that is connected back to the host processor over an ultra-wide memory bus, HBC aims to cut out the middleman by placing a small compute die at the bottom of the stack instead.

In principle, placing memory on top of a compute die has several benefits. The biggest of these is energy efficiency, as moving data around costs energy – and moving large amounts of data large distances costs even more energy. By placing memory on top of a compute die, this eliminates even the relatively short distance of an HBM connection (to say nothing of external memory like LPDDR5X), minimizing the amount of energy spent to move that data around. Those energy savings, in turn, can be funneled back into improving performance of the chip itself, or allowing a larger number of chips to be clustered together within the same energy footprint.

The compute die itself is not a full processor. But by placing the most memory bandwidth-intensive operations on the die and then sending the results from that back to the larger compute die at the center of the processor, Qualcomm is looking to get their memory and compute hardware as close together as is feasible.

Qualcomm’s efforts are also eyeing production costs here. Because of the wide memory bus used by HBM, it requires advanced packaging such as CoWoS or EMIB to connect HBM stacks to a compute die and memory controllers. But by shifting most of the computational workload to the compute die that sits under the memory, far less bandwidth is needed to connect the compute die to a larger processor die elsewhere on the chip package. And, consequently, that connection can be built with cheaper technologies such as traditional 2D organic substrates.

That said, HBC does not eliminate all of the complexity. Like HBM, it still requires bonding multiple DRAM dies (or in Qualcomm’s case: wafers) on top of another die using TSVs, which is itself a challenging process. Which means the need for complex manufacturing techniques has not gone away, but it has been reduced from both memory stacking and high speed chiplet connectivity to just the memory stacking.

Finally, Qualcomm is looking to strike a better balance between memory bandwidth and memory capacity here. Notably, the company’s HBC design calls for using LPDDR5X DRAM dies rather than the thin, high-performance dies used by HBM. The company has not outlined what the final performance of the technology will be, but the capacity of an HBC stack is already projected to be larger than what current HBM4 implementations can achieve.

Qualcomm’s fundamental argument through all of this is that HBC provides a better all-around solution than any other memory architecture, be it HBM, on-die SRAM, or off-package LPDDR. As proposed, HBC has strengths and weaknesses versus all of these technologies, but as Qualcomm argues, they can achieve memory bandwidth (and thus performance) far better than external LPDDR – and approaching HBM – without the capacity constraints of using on-die SRAM, or the high costs of the latter of those two solutions.

Ultimately, all of this is meant to lead to allowing Qualcomm to build a better chip for AI inference by meeting inference’s need for memory bandwidth and capacity with fewer drawbacks than existing technologies.
Diving into the validation process itself, for their initial HBC validation Qualcomm has hooked up an early HBC sample stack to a test unit in their San Diego labs.
While the test setup itself is not much to look at, inside of it is a chip that, for Qualcomm, is critical to their data center plans.

Given that this was an early sample, it should be noted that HBC stack they were working with here just had 2 layers of DRAM dies. Shipping products will have 4 layers. So Qualcomm is not yet at the point where they are testing full-sized stacks.

Briefly outlining their validation approach, Qualcomm tells us that they used the HBC test stack with an automated tester, which was used to measure the stack as both an LPDDR5X device and as an HBC device.

Ultimately, Qualcomm had three major findings with their successful validation testing. The first, of course, being that this worked at all, proving that it can be done. Meanwhile in regards to performance, Qualcomm measured their HBC solution as delivering more than five-times the energy efficiency (on a bandwidth-per-watt basis) than HBM4 as per its own specifications. Finally, while the company is not disclosing specific bandwidth figures, they are categorizing the measured bandwidth at 18x higher than external LPDDR5X.

The energy efficiency figure in particular is a bit short of Qualcomm’s initial projections for the technology, where they were hoping to beat HBM by 6x. But if this carries over to a full product, it still represents a significant improvement in efficiency.

According to Qualcomm, their validation testing also includes the thermal behaviors of the product, though the company has not gone into any further detail there. Qualcomm has had little to say on the subject so far, but thermal considerations are one of the major technical hurdles they will need to overcome, as a more active compute die as the base die in a stacked memory architecture is expected to put out more heat.

With their initial HBC validation complete, Qualcomm is now looking at moving on to the next step of commercialization of the technology with their Dragonfly AI250 accelerator. The successor to the Dragonfly AI200 accelerator due this year, AI250 will be the first product to integrate HBC – and it will be a key part of future Qualcomm AI accelerators after that. AI250 does not have a launch date yet, but according to Qualcomm it will begin sampling in H1 of this year, which is potentially a move-up for the company’s plans following the initial announcement that sampling would take place earlier this year.

If everything pans out with HBC, the technology will not be limited to Dragonfly AI accelerators, either. Qualcomm has previously announced that they would also be bringing the technology to their consumer-focused Snapdragon products – though the company is not specifying when and what products at the time.

Ultimately, HBC is a play for energy efficiency and a lower TCO for Qualcomm. If the technology pans out, the company expects to be able to deliver AI inference accelerators that are both more energy efficient and cheaper to build than contemporary designs. Which in turn would make them cheaper to operate (and ideally, cheaper to acquire) than GPUs for large AI inference operations. We will get to see how that plays out over the coming months as Qualcomm moves towards sampling Dragonfly AI250 in the first half of next year.

rssBodyEvidence: We checked out the ASRock Rack booth at OCP 2026 and saw servers ranging from fully integrated NVIDIA NVL72 racks to liquid-cooled switches
articles.title: Liquid-Cooled NVIDIA Servers at the ASRock Rack OCP 2026 Booth
articles.summary: We checked out the ASRock Rack booth at OCP 2026 and saw servers ranging from fully integrated NVIDIA NVL72 racks to liquid-cooled switches The post Liquid-Cooled NVIDIA Servers at the ASRock Rack OCP 2026 Booth appeared first on ServeTheHome .
bodyEvidence: At OCP Global Summit 2026 in San Jose, we stopped by the ASRock Rack booth and saw a broad set of NVIDIA systems. That included a full NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack. Next to it were HGX Rubin NVL8 servers in both 2U and 5U, two NVIDIA MGX RTX PRO servers, and a dual NVIDIA Vera CPU server. We also spotted the liquid-cooled NVIDIA Spectrum-X SN6600-LD switch and the passively cooled NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPU.
A big theme was liquid cooling. ASRock Rack used direct-to-chip liquid cooling on its rack-scale system and HGX servers, including an 8x RTX PRO 6000 PCIe server.

The XGMRACK-VR/NVL72 is ASRock Rack’s version of the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72. It is a 48RU NVIDIA MGX rack with a 5000A busbar and a liquid manifold. Inside are 18 Vera Rubin compute trays and nine NVLink 6 switch trays, for a total of 36 NVIDIA Vera CPUs and 72 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs.

NVIDIA lists the full rack at 3,600 PFLOPS of NVFP4 inference (sparse) and 2,520 PFLOPS of NVFP4 training (dense). It has 20.7TB of HBM4, and each Rubin GPU gets 288GB. Power comes from four 3RU 19″ power shelves. Each shelf is rated at 110kW and uses six 18.3kW PSUs plus bulk capacitors. ASRock Rack offers in-rack, in-row, RDHx, or liquid-to-air sidecar CDU options.

Each compute tray is a 1U NVIDIA MGX design with two Vera Rubin Superchips. Each Superchip connects two Rubin GPUs to one Vera CPU over NVLink-C2C. Networking is eight 800Gbps OSFP ports from NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, plus two 400Gbps QSFP112 ports from an NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPU. There are even management switches up top for the lower-speed networking.
The trays are fully liquid-cooled, which helps lower the total power consumption in the rack, and is something that NVIDIA has been advancing along with its partners for a few generations now.
For those who want a more traditional HGX 8-GPU form factor, there were options for that as well, but with a twist.

The 2U16X-GNR2/DLC RUBIN was one of the most impressive systems at the booth. It puts an NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 board, with eight Rubin GPUs, into a 2U chassis. It is fully liquid-cooled, covering the E1.S drives, CPUs, and GPUs, with no fans. Networking includes NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs and BlueField-4 DPUs. Power comes in over a 54V DC busbar.

The host is a dual-socket Intel Xeon 6 platform. It supports the Xeon 6700P, 6500P, and 6700E series in LGA 4710 sockets, with 16+16 DIMM slots at 2DPC. While it supports other series, given the cost of the rest of the system, we would imagine the vast majority of folks buying these will opt for the Xeon 6700P series.
There are eight 800Gbps OSFP ports via NVIDIA ConnectX-9, along with 8x hot-swap E1.S NVMe bays. NVIDIA quotes 400 PFLOPS of NVFP4 compute (sparse) for HGX Rubin NVL8.
The HGX 8-GPU platform underwent major changes in this generation, including a change in GPU orientation in the tray. This change enables it to work in high-density, liquid-cooled racks.
There was more in the booth, including hybrid-cooled servers, so let us get to those next.

rssBodyEvidence: As production hardware starts shipping, NVIDIA has updated some of the specifications for its Rubin GPU platforms
articles.title: NVIDIA Updates Rubin GPU Specs as First Production Hardware Arrives
articles.summary: As production hardware starts shipping, NVIDIA has updated some of the specifications for its Rubin GPU platforms The post NVIDIA Updates Rubin GPU Specs as First Production Hardware Arrives appeared first on ServeTheHome .
bodyEvidence: As we roll into the fourth quarter of 2026, NVIDIA and its partners are in the middle of the Vera Rubin ramp-up, including hyperscalers making some of the first NVL72 systems generally available to their customers . With Vera Rubin reaching the tipping point of its production roll-out, NVIDIA is also finally locking down the hardware shipping specifications. As it turns out, the company has quietly revised those specifications, with the Rubin GPU now offering less memory and scale-up networking (NVLink) bandwidth than NVIDIA previously promoted, but more scale-out bandwidth.

As initially spotted by IT Home , back in September NVIDIA posted the updated specifications for its Rubin GPU and various Rubin-based products on their webpages and in NVIDIA’s architecture datasheet. To be sure, it is not unusual for server hardware specifications to change before a product’s launch, especially for something like Vera Rubin, which was announced nearly a year in advance. NVIDIA’s case is no different, with the company previously noting that those specifications were preliminary and that “all values are up to and subject to change” at the time.

First, let us talk about NVIDIA’s Rubin GPU. The cornerstone of NVIDIA’s ambitions for this generation, NVIDIA’s Rubin server GPU will find its way into systems big and small and serve as the building block for much larger projects.

Compared to NVIDIA’s preliminary specifications, the HBM4 memory bandwidth for a single Rubin GPU has been revised down notably. NVIDIA was initially targeting 22TB/second of memory bandwidth per Rubin GPU. At 8 stacks of HBM4 memory, that meant running each stack at about 10.75Gbps/pin. But with these revised shipping specifications, a single Rubin GPU will now provide 19.2TB/second of bandwidth, for a data rate of about 9.375Gbps/pin, a net loss of 1.375Gbps, or roughly 11%.

This spec change comes as NVIDIA has been projecting some very aggressive data rates for HBM4. The super-sized version of the high-bandwidth memory specification already doubled the memory bus width per stack from 1024 bits to 2048 bits. At the same time, the official specification called for HBM4 stacks to run at a slightly lower clock rate than HBM3E, targeting 8Gbps/pin. NVIDIA’s 10.75Gbps rate was significantly higher than the original HBM4 specification, and even their newly reduced 9.375Gbps data rate is still quite a bit above.

For context, NVIDIA’s rival AMD will run its HBM4 stacks on the MI455X at only 7.6Gbps/pin . So NVIDIA’s revised targets are significantly higher than those of some other HBM4 consumers. Even after the news broke, NVIDIA has not said why it revised the memory bandwidth specs down. In lieu of that, the immediate assumption is that NVIDIA and its memory partners cannot deliver on those specs, be it memory controller speeds, memory stack speeds, memory stack yields (how many can run at the desired speed), or perhaps a combination of all of those factors. Regardless of the reason, the net result is that customers will have less GPU memory bandwidth at their disposal, with performance ramifications.

NVLink interconnect bandwidth is also taking a hit compared to NVIDIA’s original expectations. The preliminary specification for NVIDIA’s multi-GPU connection and scale-up fabric was for 3.6TB/second of NVLink bandwidth for each Rubin GPU. That is now a flat 3.0TB/second, a 600GB/second (or 17%) reduction. NVLink is an area where NVIDIA pushes hard to make many physical GPUs act as one, so it usually pushes the limits of what is possible.

While NVLink (scale-up) bandwidth has been reduced, scale-out networking bandwidth is now overperforming. For a single Rubin GPU, NVIDIA is offering 450GB/second of networking bandwidth, up from their preliminary specification of 400GB/second.

Beyond these changes, NVIDIA has not changed any other specifications for Rubin GPUs. The theoretical (on paper) compute throughput remains unchanged at 50 PFLOPS of FP4 inference and 35 PFLOPS of FP4 training. So NVIDIA has hit its clock speed and memory-capacity targets for the GPU.

Rubin’s spec changes will also affect all the products it will go into, most notably NVIDIA’s flagship Vera Rubin NVL72 rack. NVL72 showcases all of NVIDIA’s technologies, integrating its Vera CPUs, BlueField-4 DPUs, and, of course, Rubin GPUs.

For NVL72, its specifications have been revised in lockstep with the changes to a single Rubin GPU. That means that cumulative GPU memory bandwidth has gone from 1,580TB/second to 1400TB/second for the rack-scale system, a net loss of 180 TB (11%). Though, as with a single Rubin, the GPU memory capacity for NVL72 remains unchanged at 20.7TB of HBM4.

NVLink bandwidth across the system for its scale-up domain has also been adjusted. NVIDIA’s plans to offer 260TB/second of bandwidth across the rack have been revised down to 216TB/second, a 17% reduction matching the new 3TB/second rate of each Rubin GPU.

The silver lining for NVL72 is that it gets the same scale-out networking bandwidth boost as the individual Rubin chips. So whereas NVL72 was originally slated to offer 28.8TB/second of networking bandwidth, that has been dialed up to 32.4TB/second (bidirectional). This means that for larger deployments that make heavy use of scale-out networking, more bandwidth (and ideally, more performance) is now available than NVIDIA first projected.

Past this, the rest of the figures for Vera Rubin NVL72 remain unchanged from the earlier specifications. Whether an NVL72 rack can hit quite the same level of AI performance with less memory and NVLink bandwidth as originally intended seems doubtful, but the GPU compute hardware (and its CPU counterpart) is shipping at spec.

Finally, separate from the specification changes to the base Rubin GPU and the NVL72 rack, NVIDIA has also revised its other products built from Rubin. This includes the Vera Rubin Superchip, the Vera Rubin NVL4, and the HGX Rubin NVL8 products. The last one is getting a special mention here because, on top of the Rubin spec changes, it is getting a further change of its own.

On top of GPU memory bandwidth and NVLink bandwidth reductions, NVIDIA is also cutting back the amount of HBM4 memory available in NVL8 systems. These systems were originally set to come with 2.3TB of HBM4, but that is now down to a flat 2.0TB, losing 300GB (or 13%) of GPU memory.

NVIDIA’s preliminary figure would require each Rubin GPU in an NVL8 to be a full Rubin with its complete complement of 288GB of HBM4 available. However, a 2.0TB setup means each GPU needs only around 250GB of HBM4 available. That, in turn, requires only 7 of the GPU’s 8 HBM4 memory stacks.

Consequently, NVL8 is taking the biggest memory bandwidth hit of the entire Rubin family. Rather than losing just 11% of its memory bandwidth, it is losing 26%, or about 46TB/second. Each Rubin GPU would only have 250GB to 252GB of memory available, for 16.8TB/second of bandwidth per GPU.

Inference performance remains unchanged, at 400 PFLOPS for FP4, but FP4 training performance has been reduced from 280 PFLOPS to 270, and FP8 training has similarly been dialed down from 140 PFLOPS to 130. The 8-way Rubin systems do get the same network bandwidth improvement as the rest of the Rubin lineup. That figure has gone from 1.6TB/second to 1.8TB/second.

Finally, these changes affect both versions of the HGX NVL8, as well as DGX systems based on the NVL8 platform. Both the HGX Rubin NVL8 (Rubin + x86 CPU) and the HGX Vera Rubin NVL8 (Rubin + Vera) are subject to the same GPU changes.

It seems NVIDIA has had to rein in its ambitions for the Rubin GPU to bring the product to market at the scale they are aiming for, dialing back both GPU HBM4 memory bandwidth and NVLink networking bandwidth. The full ramifications of these changes are unclear at this time since not all workloads are bottlenecked by memory or networking bandwidth in the same way. In some respects, it is academic, since these changes apply to all shipping Rubin hardware from day one. Still, there will be a lot of NVIDIA Rubin deployed over the next few quarters.

rssBodyEvidence: SambaNova and Supermicro will build and sell disaggregated inference systems that pair NVIDIA GPUs with SambaNova’s SN50 Reconfigurable Dataflow Units (RDUs), with Supermicro initially planning for 10,000 SN50 chips. The racks join Supermicro’s Data Center Building Block Solutions (DCBBS) catalog, and Supermicro will integrate, test, deliver, and support them. Both companies describe the 10,000 chips as a planning figure for a phased rollout; neither has disclosed a purchase commitment, pricing, or a ship date.

The split follows the two phases of LLM inference. Prefill processes the prompt and is compute-bound, which SambaNova assigns to the NVIDIA GPUs; decode generates the response one token at a time and is memory-bound, which it assigns to the SN50. SambaNova’s case for the pairing is that agentic workloads spend most of their time in decode, because an agent makes thousands of model calls and each response gates its next action, so a faster decode stage shortens the whole loop.

SN50 is SambaNova’s fifth-generation RDU, and the company says it serves the largest models at high throughput without extreme rack power density, so operators can add inference capacity in existing facilities and keep GPUs they already own on prefill duty. SambaNova claims 5x the compute per accelerator and 4x the network bandwidth of its previous generation for the SambaRack SN50, which is air-cooled and scales to 256 accelerators.

SambaRack SN50 carries 16 RDUs per rack, so the initial 10,000-chip plan works out to about 625 racks if Supermicro keeps that density. SambaNova has not published throughput, latency, or power figures for the combined GPU and RDU systems, and Supermicro has not specified the server configurations, GPU models, or interconnects, or how many GPUs and RDUs each system holds. Supermicro’s DCBBS catalog already includes the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 racks and the Vera CPU rack it positions for agent sandboxes.

Supermicro takes system integration, testing, delivery, and customer support, including on-site service, while SambaNova engineers bring models onto SN50, tune them for the hardware, and assist Supermicro with deployments. For buyers, the change is in the channel: SN50 RDUs can be ordered alongside GPUs from Supermicro in the same way as the rest of a rack, with one vendor responsible for the system.

“Agentic AI is the next wave of inference, and it has to run everywhere,” said Rodrigo Liang, co-founder and CEO of SambaNova. “Supermicro builds AI infrastructure for data centers globally. Now customers can order SN50 RDUs alongside GPUs, from a world-leading partner they trust. That’s how fast, efficient inference gets to scale.”

“Our collaboration with SambaNova expands our broad DCBBS portfolio by enabling heterogeneous architectures that integrate GPU computing with specialized inference acceleration, helping customers deploy efficient, scalable AI solutions,” said Charles Liang, president and CEO of Supermicro.

The companies will start with NeoClouds and sovereign clouds, then expand to enterprises running AI on premises. SambaNova expects the partnership to put substantially more high-performance inference capacity into service in 2027 than it could alone, and it has not named customers or given a schedule for the 10,000 chips. The deal follows SambaNova’s July first close of a $1 billion financing at an $11 billion valuation, which came with JPMorganChase deploying SN40 and SN50 systems for on-prem inference, and its heterogeneous inference collaboration with Intel.

rssBodyEvidence: Broadcom today updated the VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) portfolio with two new Advanced Services, VMware Live Recovery and VMware Compliance and Configuration Management, and introduced VMware vSphere Express, a 128-core package built on vSphere 9 for smaller environments. The update also lays out the next VCF release, planned for Broadcom’s fiscal first quarter of 2027, with automated AI infrastructure deployment, native S3-compatible object storage on vSAN, infrastructure compliance management, policy-based VPC connectivity, and native disaster recovery.

Two of the capabilities Broadcom highlights shipped with VCF 9.1.1, which reached general availability on September 3 and which we covered from VMware Explore 2026 . Multi-tenant Model Sharing lets several internal business units consume one centrally deployed Model Runtime stack while keeping per-tenant data privacy, security boundaries, and isolated context. Broadcom says sharing the deployment cuts GPU count and infrastructure cost against running a model stack per tenant, and it has not published GPU savings or cost figures for the claim.

Confidential computing, which Broadcom lists as generally available in VCF 9.1.1, encrypts data in use at the hardware level on AMD and Intel platforms, with AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX as the supported implementations. Broadcom says it protects workloads against CPU vulnerability exploitation, VM-cloning data exfiltration, and cross-tenant data leakage, and cryptographic attestation confirms a workload is running untampered. The company positions it for regulated, sovereign cloud, and AI workloads where data privacy is the deciding requirement.

AI Infrastructure Quickstart, planned for the next release, automates the setup of private AI infrastructure through a vCenter plugin that handles vCenter cluster deployment, Supervisor configuration, and vSphere Kubernetes Service cluster provisioning. Broadcom calls it an automated Day 0 deployment and has not given deployment-time figures. The company’s fiscal first quarter of 2027 runs through the start of February, so the release is about a quarter out if the estimate holds.

vSAN native S3-compatible object storage, which entered VCF 9.1.1 as a tech preview, is planned to reach general availability in the same release. It provides object storage inside VCF for AI projects, cloud-native applications, and backup and recovery workloads, with self-service provisioning through vSphere Supervisor or VCF Automation, so a VCF tenant can create buckets without a separate object storage platform.

VCF infrastructure configuration management and compliance, planned as a native feature inside VCF Operations in the next release, monitors VCF component settings against benchmarks including the Payment Card Industry (PCI) standard and the VCF Security Baseline, with configuration drift detection and remediation for components such as vCenter and VCF Storage. Broadcom frames it as a move from reactive to proactive compliance management for the platform itself.

Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) policy-based connectivity, scheduled for the same release, lets platform engineers define shared services, workload isolation, and security policies once and apply them across environments, while developers consume network resources through self-service without manual approvals. Native disaster recovery is planned for both VCF and VMware vSphere Foundation (VVF), orchestrating recovery across thousands of workloads after power outages, hardware failures, natural disasters, and human error; Broadcom has not published recovery time or recovery point objectives for it.

VMware HyperArmor, announced at Explore on Tour Frankfurt, is now on the Advanced Services list as a real-time defense layer for the ESX hypervisor in VCF. It applies virtual patches to mitigate vulnerabilities before a host is patched, monitors the hypervisor continuously with positive security guardrails that block unauthorized software, and adds multi-factor authentication to the SSH login path so a stolen password alone does not grant access.

VMware Live Recovery joins the catalog today with disaster and cyber recovery for VMware workloads, integrated with VCF. In the on-premises cyber recovery workflow, protected VMs replicate from the primary site across an air gap into an isolated clean room on vSAN, where VM network isolation and endpoint detection and response scanning run before workloads return to production. Broadcom says iterative recovery and enterprise-scale orchestration lower the cost of running separate recovery tools.

VMware Compliance and Configuration Management is the second service added today. It is built on the VMware Salt remote execution engine, which Broadcom previously sold inside VMware Advanced Cyber Compliance and now offers on its own, and it enforces compliance for VM and container workloads with event-driven detection of unauthorized file changes or exposed ports and automated remediation. Supported benchmarks include the Center for Internet Security (CIS), the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA), and customer-defined standards, and it is separate from the infrastructure compliance feature planned inside VCF Operations.

VMware vSphere Express is available now in all regions. Built on vSphere 9, it is a 128-core package for smaller environments that includes vMotion, High Availability, Distributed Switch, vCenter Quick Patch, and TPM 2.0 and vTPM 2.0 support, and Broadcom has not published pricing. For the European Economic Area, Broadcom will keep vSphere Standard 8 and vSphere Enterprise Plus 8 on sale until October 31, 2027, with extended support on active subscriptions until the subscription ends or October 31, 2028, whichever comes first.

rssBodyEvidence: Simplyblock’s Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver and Kubernetes operator now carry Red Hat certification and are listed in the Red Hat Ecosystem Catalog, which gives OpenShift Virtualization customers a validated storage layer for VMs moved off VMware vSphere. The software-defined platform runs on servers customers already own, provisions NVMe block volumes for containers and KubeVirt VMs, and includes the replication and disaster recovery features simplyblock added to the platform in September.

Simplyblock runs as a distributed storage engine inside Kubernetes, pooling NVMe devices across nodes into one block storage pool that serves both containerized services and KubeVirt VMs. Hosts reach volumes over NVMe/TCP or NVMe over RDMA (RoCEv2), and the I/O path is built on the Storage Performance Development Kit (SPDK), which runs in user space to avoid the Linux kernel’s storage overhead. Simplyblock targets sub-millisecond latency and grows capacity by adding nodes to the cluster.

Data is protected with distributed erasure coding, which simplyblock says provides the fault tolerance of three-way mirroring at lower raw cost: a 4+2 scheme stores usable capacity at 1.5x raw against 3x for triple replication. The platform also handles thin provisioning, copy-on-write snapshots, writable clones, per-tenant quality of service limits, and volume-level encryption. The Red Hat Ecosystem Catalog lists five certified simplyblock container images, with the operator bundle at version 26.3.0 supporting OpenShift 4.19 through 4.22 and the CSI driver at 26.2.4.

The replication and recovery features simplyblock added in September are part of the certified stack. Synchronous replication across a metro-distance stretch cluster delivers a zero recovery point objective (RPO), and asynchronous replication between clusters reaches RPOs as low as one minute, with delta-based transfers and automated failback. Live forward replication moves running volumes, including VM disks, between clusters without disruption, and point-in-time backups go to any S3-compatible object store for off-site protection.

Simplyblock CEO Rob Pankow says organizations leaving VMware need an OpenShift storage design that covers what vSAN, vMotion, and Site Recovery Manager did for them, and that certified storage with integrated disaster recovery provides it without a separately licensed DR product.

rssBodyEvidence: The AMD Instinct MI350P is AMD’s first new PCIe Instinct GPU in four years, following the MI210 in 2022. It brings the company’s CDNA 4 architecture to a conventional add-in card, with up to 4.6 PFLOPS of MXFP4 performance, 144GB of HBM3E, and 4TB/s of memory bandwidth. All of that fits into a dual-slot, 600W air-cooled card, giving customers another way to deploy Instinct GPUs without moving to the larger 8 GPU OAM MI350/5X platform.

AMD also showcased the MI350P at IFA 2026 in its Threadripper Halo Station prototype, where the same accelerators were liquid-cooled. The workstation concept supports up to four MI350Ps alongside a 96-core Threadripper PRO processor, providing 576GB of aggregate HBM3E capacity in a single machine; AMD’s product page, updated in October, now lists the system as coming in 2027. That gives us two ways to look at the MI350P: as a PCIe accelerator for servers, and as the building block for a larger deskside AI system competing with machines like the GB300 DGX Station.

This first look takes the server view, so the comparison that matters for a buyer specifying a PCIe accelerator is the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, the card that sits in the same power class and the same slots, and the H200 NVL is in the charts as the most capable NVIDIA add-in card for the workloads where memory bandwidth decides the result. A single GB300 DGX Station stands in for the deskside view; it is a different class of machine at a different price, and it is there to show how far a full Blackwell Ultra GPU sits above any of the PCIe cards.

AMD’s published numbers put the MI350P’s weight on low precision: 4.6 PFLOPS at MXFP4 and MXFP6, 2.3 PFLOPS at FP8, and 1.15 PFLOPS at FP16 or BF16, all dense figures. The memory system is the other half of the card: 144GB of HBM3E on a 4,096-bit interface at 4TB/s, behind a 128MB Infinity Cache, which is what the single-stream results below lean on. Board power is 600W with a 450W configurable mode; our review unit ran at 450W.

The MI350P uses the same CDNA 4 architecture as the larger, higher-power MI350/5X GPUs. The MI350P can be thought of as effectively half of a MI350X. To understand why, it helps to look at how the larger GPU is assembled.

The MI350X is a 3D-stacked chiplet design built on TSMC’s CoWoS, or Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate, packaging, with no single monolithic die. Eight accelerator complex dies, or XCDs, sit above two I/O dies, with four XCDs on each I/O die. AMD’s Infinity Fabric connects the chiplets, while eight HBM3E stacks provide the GPU’s memory. CoWoS describes the package-level integration; the compute-over-I/O arrangement is the design’s vertical, 3D-stacked component.

The MI350P takes one half of that arrangement: four XCDs, one I/O die, and four HBM3E stacks. Each XCD has 32 active compute units, giving the card 128 CUs compared with the MI350X’s 256. The memory resources are also halved: 144GB of HBM3E against 288GB, 4TB/s of bandwidth against 8TB/s, and 128MB of Infinity Cache against 256MB.

The 600W figure is a maximum, and AMD lets the card be configured down to 450W, which is where it ran in our 2U host. The H200 NVL matched it at 450W in the R770, but the RTX PRO 6000 ran at its full 600W in the XE7740, so the NVIDIA card had 150W more to work with in every comparison against it. The full-power results wait for a chassis that can cool a 600W passive card, and Dell’s XE7745 technical guide lists eight MI350Ps at 600W.
The other note: the single 12V-2×6 connector and the 10.5-inch, double-slot board, which is what lets the card go into the same risers that hold an RTX PRO 6000 or an H200 NVL today.

The table below sets the MI350P beside the three NVIDIA systems in our charts: the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, which shares its slot, its power range, and its PCIe 5.0 x16 host link; the H200 NVL, the Hopper card with the memory bandwidth to match it; and the GB300 DGX Station, a single Blackwell Ultra GPU paired with a Grace CPU over NVLink-C2C.

The rows to read first are memory capacity, where the MI350P’s 144GB is the largest of the three PCIe cards, 3GB above the H200 NVL and 48GB above the RTX PRO 6000; memory bandwidth, where its 4TB/s sits between the two; and the FP4 line, where AMD quotes a dense figure, and NVIDIA quotes sparse.

Against the RTX PRO 6000, the MI350P’s memory subsystem is the most immediate difference. It has 50 percent more GPU memory and roughly 2.5x the memory bandwidth. For a model that doesn’t fit comfortably within 96GB, the additional capacity could determine whether it runs on one GPU or needs to be distributed across several.

The RTX PRO 6000, however, serves a broader range of workloads, with hardware for graphics, ray tracing, and video alongside its AI capabilities. The choice weighs more than two peak compute figures; it also depends on what else the system needs to do.

The H200 NVL is the more direct comparison for the MI350P among high-memory PCIe accelerators; the larger Blackwell datacenter GPUs sit in a different class. Memory capacity is nearly identical at 144GB versus the H200’s 141GB, with both using HBM3E, and the H200 offers 20 percent more memory bandwidth at 4.8TB/s. The two also scale differently: all three PCIe cards connect to the host over PCIe, but the H200 NVL adds dedicated GPU-to-GPU connectivity through NVLink bridges connecting up to four GPUs.

The larger MI350X and MI355X were built to compete with Blackwell, but the MI350P cuts that hardware configuration in half. That brings it closer to the H200 NVL in memory attributes and in overall positioning. One place where the MI350P still distinguishes itself is native MXFP4 and MXFP6 support, which matters more as inference moves toward lower precision.

The smaller memory subsystem is another compromise, because AMD has not offset the reduction in HBM stacks with faster HBM3E, leaving the MI350P at 4TB/s of bandwidth and behind the H200 NVL on this metric. That can limit performance in memory-bandwidth-bound workloads, regardless of the available compute, as the memory bandwidth and long-prompt inference results later in the review show.

The DGX Station comparison runs the other way, because the GB300 Station carries a full B300 GPU with one HBM stack disabled, a datacenter-class chip on a datacenter power budget, while the MI350P is half of a datacenter-class chip fitted into the 600W envelope of a PCIe add-in card. AMD needs two or four MI350Ps to meet that single GPU, and on paper two of them do: 288GB and 8TB/s against the Station’s 252GB and 7.1TB/s. Those resources sit on two cards, though, and a workload spanning both exchanges data over PCIe peer-to-peer, which limits how much the second card adds.

The MI350P review unit is a Dell PowerEdge R7725 with two AMD EPYC 9555 processors (64 cores each), 1.5TB of DDR5-6400 across 24 DIMMs, and two MI350P cards set to 450W, the cap for a 2U server. The RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition cards (600W) ran in the Dell PowerEdge XE7740 that carries our four-card inference build, a single H200 NVL (450W) ran in the Dell PowerEdge R770 from our review, and the GB300 figures come from the ASUS ExpertCenter Pro ET900N G3 DGX Station we reviewed in September.

The iDRAC inventory below shows how the two cards are seated. They sit in PCIe slots 2 and 7, both Gen5 x16 and both reporting healthy, and the device keys, 0-139-0 and 1-199-0, read to us as one card behind each EPYC socket, so tensor-parallel traffic between the two MI350Ps crosses the socket link on its way between root complexes. That is the layout a two-card deployment in a 2U server gets by default, and it is worth keeping in mind on the two-card results later.

The memory view shows the rest of the host: 24 DIMMs of 64GB DDR5-6400, dual rank, for 1,536GB in a server that tops out at 6TB, all with multi-bit ECC. The headroom matters for the GLM-5.2 run, where the MXFP4 checkpoint does not fit in two cards’ 288GB and vLLM offloads part of the expert weights to host memory.

To put the MI350P’s compute in context, we ran MAMF across the four systems. MAMF (Maximum Achievable Matmul FLOPS) is a practical performance metric designed to measure the realistic peak floating-point operations per second an accelerator reaches during matrix multiplication, a more useful benchmark than the theoretical peak FLOPS in the spec sheet. We sweep each system in BF16, FP8, and block-scaled FP4 and report the best sustained dense result per precision; the hatched bars multiply each PCIe card’s result by the card count used in the large-model serving runs and are calculated, with no measurement behind them.

At 450W, one MI350P reaches 580 TFLOPS in BF16, 1,120 in FP8, and 2,228 in FP4. The RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell follows at 419, 820, and 1,634, so the MI350P holds a 36 to 38 percent lead over the NVIDIA card at every precision while running 150W below it, with the widest gap in BF16 at 38.4 percent.

The H200 NVL’s 652 TFLOPS in BF16 and 1,205 in FP8 put it ahead of the MI350P on both, and it has no FP4 path. The GB300 DGX Station sits above all three PCIe cards at 1,924, 3,802, and 6,024, roughly 3.3x the MI350P at BF16 and 2.7x at FP4; two MI350Ps on paper close to 1,160 and 4,456, still short of the Station’s single GPU. The NVIDIA MAMF figures in this review come from our latest runs on each card and replace the results from our earlier testing.

Raw compute throughput is only useful if the accelerator can keep its execution units supplied with data. This matters most for inference, where token generation during the decode phase is limited more by memory bandwidth than by available FLOPS. The bandwidth test reads, writes, and copies GPU memory through compute kernels and the copy engine, showing the bandwidth available inside each GPU against its rated figure.

One MI350P reads its HBM3E at 3,291GB/s and writes at 3,204GB/s, about 80 percent of the 4TB/s rating, with copies at 1,276 to 1,283GB/s; a copy consumes bandwidth twice, once to read the source and again to write the destination. The RTX PRO 6000’s GDDR7 manages 1,540GB/s on reads and 1,483GB/s on writes, so the MI350P carries about 2.1x the usable bandwidth per card.

The H200 NVL’s 4,472GB/s read and 4,156GB/s write figures run 36 and 30 percent ahead of the MI350P, in line with its 4.8TB/s rating against 4TB/s, and the GB300 DGX Station reaches 6,869GB/s. Two MI350Ps measured together reach 6,529GB/s on reads, near the Station, but that bandwidth sits in two PCIe slots, and a model spanning both pays for every exchange over PCIe.

With the low-level tests covered, we move to LLM inference. Our vLLM online serving test drives an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with a fixed number of concurrent streams and records output tokens per second across the run. We report two shapes: 512 tokens in and 512 out, which is chat-sized and decode-heavy, and 8,192 in and 1,024 out, which is RAG- and document-sized and leans on prefill. Concurrency doubles from one stream upward, and each chart stops at the highest concurrency at which every card in it completed. Every point is two requests per stream, so single-stream figures rest on two requests and carry more run-to-run variance than the higher-concurrency points.

Each model ran on the fewest cards that could hold it: one MI350P for everything through GPT-OSS-120B and MiniMax-M2.7, and two for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, MiniMax-M3, GLM-5.2, and GLM-5.3 Flash. The RTX PRO 6000 runs follow the same rule, which puts two RTX cards against one MI350P on MiniMax-M2.7 and four against two on MiniMax-M3 and GLM-5.2. Low-precision builds differ by vendor: AMD’s are MXFP4 through Quark, NVIDIA’s are NVFP4, and the FP4 pairings are labeled that way throughout. GPT-OSS ships as MXFP4 and runs the same weights on every card. The H200 NVFP4 builds are not included.

Read down the MI350P column, and the card count is the first thing 144GB gets you. Six of the ten models run on one MI350P, where the RTX PRO 6000’s 96GB needs a second card for MiniMax-M2.7, and the two MXFP4 checkpoints that stay on a pair of MI350Ps, MiniMax-M3 and GLM-5.2, need four RTX PRO 6000s. GLM-5.2 is the one that outgrows even 288GB, and vLLM offloads part of its expert weights to the R7725’s host memory for that run; the GB300 does the same with about 215GB of experts in Grace memory.

The MI350P figures for the single-card models were run October 27 on AMDGPU 31.60, ROCm 10.1.0, and vLLM 0.32.0. Dell’s validated combination is vLLM 0.27 with ROCm 10.0 and AMDGPU 31.5, and we went one step past it to the ROCm 10.1 release of October 5. The NVIDIA cards ran the vLLM 26.08 container on CUDA 13.4.1 throughout. The table lists the build behind each run.

The four two-card models, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, MiniMax-M3, GLM-5.2, and GLM-5.3 Flash, are reported from runs on ROCm 7.2.3. Our ROCm 10.1 passes on those models used CPU expert offload throughout and, on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, a speculative decoder the NVIDIA runs did not, which makes them a different test, so they are held for a clean pass on the current stack, and the tables label every MI350P row with its stack.

AMD’s preferred path for these models is its AIM containers; the Enterprise AI Suite 2.5 release of October 9 is validated on ROCm 10 and carries AIMs for GPT-OSS-120B, Llama 3.3 70B, and Gemma 3 27B, but AMD’s accelerator table lists an optimized MI350P profile only for Wan2.2 so far. Stock vLLM is therefore still the path an MI350P buyer takes today, and is what we measured.

There are 28 charts below, so here is the short version in two tables: output tokens per second for each model at the highest concurrency every card completed, with the chat-sized 512-in, 512-out workload first. The MI350P figures are one card at 450W unless the row says otherwise, with a column for the stack each row comes from; the GB300 DGX Station is a single B300.

Two results stand out in the chat table: the MI350P beats the RTX PRO 6000 on every FP8, BF16, and GPT-OSS model, by 35 to 65 percent at 128 streams, trails NVIDIA’s NVFP4 builds only at the top of the Llama and MiniMax-M2.7 curves, and roughly doubles the NVIDIA card at a single stream on Llama 3.1 8B and Mistral Small 24B, where 4TB/s of HBM3E does the work.

The H200 NVL, with 20 percent more bandwidth, stays 4 to 18 percent ahead on the dense FP8 and BF16 models at 128 streams and ties on Llama 3.1 8B FP8; on the two GPT-OSS models the order reverses, and the MI350P finishes 50 and 78 percent ahead.
The second table repeats the exercise on the 8,192-token prompts, where prefill dominates the run and the balance between compute and memory bandwidth shifts toward the NVIDIA cards.

On prefill-heavy prompts, the picture is mixed: the MI350P leads the RTX PRO 6000 on both GPT-OSS models at every stream count and on Mistral Small, splits Qwen3-Coder at 128 streams (24 percent ahead on BF16, 8 percent behind on FP8), and flattens by 16 streams on Llama and MiniMax-M2.7, where it finishes behind the NVIDIA card. Against the H200, it leads on GPT-OSS by 15 percent on the 120B model and 5 percent on the 20B at 128 streams and trails by 25 to 58 percent on the dense models.

On the largest models, where two MI350Ps face four RTX PRO 6000s, the NVIDIA set leads GLM-5.2 through 16 streams on the chat workload with 384GB of GDDR7 against 288GB of HBM3E, while on MiniMax-M3 all three configurations stay within 10 percent through eight streams before the RTX quad pulls ahead at 16. The single GB300 clears every PCIe configuration by a wide margin on anything that fits in its 252GB.

GLM-5.3 Flash was not run on the RTX PRO 6000, so the comparison is two MI350P cards against the single GB300 Station through 32 streams. On the chat workload, the MI350P pair starts behind, 45 against 353 output tokens per second at one stream, and crosses the Station at eight streams on its way to 1,462 at 32, against 828 for the Station. On the prefill-heavy workload the Station leads throughout, 1,219 against 760 at 32 streams, where the pair’s prefill has to cross PCIe between the two cards and the B300 does it all in one piece of HBM.

GLM-5.2 is the memory story in this set. The MXFP4 checkpoint spills past the two MI350P cards’ 288GB into host memory, so single-stream throughput is 2 output tokens per second on the pair against 9 for four RTX PRO 6000 cards holding the NVFP4 build in 384GB of GDDR7 and 35 for the Station, which offloads about 215GB of expert weights to Grace memory. The RTX quad leads through 16 streams on the chat workload; at 32 the MI350P pair reaches 59 against 40, and the Station reaches 139. On prefill-heavy prompts, neither PCIe configuration gets past single digits through 16 streams, against 87 for the Station.

Two MI350Ps hold the MXFP4 build of MiniMax-M3 in 288GB; the NVIDIA side needs four RTX PRO 6000 cards. The three configurations run within 10 percent of each other through eight streams on the chat workload; the RTX quad pulls ahead at 16 (1,181 against 998 for the pair and 940 for the Station), and at 32 the MI350P pair reads 1,509 against 759 for the quad and 1,041 for the Station.

On prefill-heavy prompts, the MI350P pair leads at every point through eight streams, 524 against 444 for the quad, while the Station, which keeps a slice of this model’s experts in Grace memory, falls to 103.

With two cards on each side and the native FP8 checkpoint, the RTX PRO 6000 pair leads through eight streams on the chat workload and the MI350P pair takes over from 16, finishing at 1,081 against 829 at 32 streams; the single Station reaches 1,766 at the same point. The prefill-heavy run follows the same shape, the MI350P pair at 621 against 345 for the RTX pair at 32 streams and 954 for the Station.

One MI350P carries the MXFP4 build of MiniMax-M2.7 against two RTX PRO 6000 cards on NVFP4. The single MI350P leads the pair at one stream (124 against 115), stays 8 to 20 percent ahead through 64 streams 1,486 against 1,339, then flattens at 1,524 at 128 and 1,557 at 256, while the RTX pair continues to 1,932 and 2,842; the Station reaches 4,793.
On the prefill-heavy workload, the MI350P holds at 304 to 331 output tokens per second from eight streams through 64, against 501 for the RTX pair and 1,744 for the Station.

GPT-OSS ships as MXFP4, so every card runs the same weights. One MI350P leads one RTX PRO 6000 at every stream count on both workloads, by 40 to 93 percent from four streams up, and finishes at 5,057 output tokens per second on the chat workload and 2,101 on prefill-heavy prompts at 128 streams, against 3,064 and 1,169 for the RTX PRO 6000 and 3,376 and 1,825 for the H200 NVL; the Station reaches 9,280 and 5,023.

AMD and Dell’s MLPerf Inference v6.1 submission of September 16 puts a ceiling on the same model: eight MI350Ps in a PowerEdge XE7745 produced 48,971 tokens per second offline and 40,868 in the server scenario on GPT-OSS-120B, which is 6,121 and 5,108 per GPU, on a tuned submission stack. That harness and ours are not like-for-like, but the 5,057 we measured at 128 streams on stock vLLM sits at the bottom of that range.

The smaller OpenAI model follows the same curve. The MI350P leads the RTX PRO 6000 at every point, 8,174 against 4,992 at 64 streams and 10,726 against 7,937 at 128 on the chat workload, and 3,460 against 2,083 and 3,603 against 2,482 on prefill-heavy prompts, and it runs to 16,406 at 256 streams where the RTX PRO 6000 reads 11,077. The H200 NVL trails the MI350P on both shapes, at 6,022 and 3,419 at 128 streams, and the Station sits at 22,041 and 9,555.

The 30B MoE with 3B active parameters gives the MI350P a lead over the RTX PRO 6000 at every concurrency on the chat workload, finishing at 6,451 against 3,995 on FP8 and 4,696 against 2,881 on BF16 at 128 streams, with the H200 at 7,459 and 5,240.

On prefill-heavy prompts, the FP8 run leads only through four streams and then trails the RTX PRO 6000 from eight through 128, 759 against 823 at the top, with the H200 at 1,820; the BF16 run climbs to 728 at 128 streams against 588 and 1,592.

Mistral Small is the MI350P’s strongest dense result against the RTX PRO 6000: 4,458 against 3,242 on FP8 and 3,065 against 2,026 on BF16 at 128 streams on the chat workload, and at one stream the MI350P roughly doubles the NVIDIA card (100 against 56 on FP8, 67 against 32 on BF16).

It is also the dense model where the MI350P leads on prefill-heavy prompts, 599 against 482 on FP8 at 128 streams and 425 against 299 on BF16 at 64, though the H200 reaches 799 and 632 at the same points.

Llama 3.1 8B is here for continuity with our older GPU coverage. At 128 streams on the chat workload, the MI350P delivers 11,045 output tokens per second on FP8 against 8,073 for the RTX PRO 6000 and 11,054 for the H200, a tie with the Hopper card, and 6,819 on BF16 against 4,740 and 8,069. AMD’s MXFP4 build reaches 8,383 at 128 streams, 5 percent behind NVIDIA’s NVFP4 build on the RTX PRO 6000 (8,869), after leading it by 12 to 143 percent at every lower stream count; at a single stream the MXFP4 run reads 323 against 133.

The prefill-heavy runs invert the result: MI350P FP8 flattens by 16 streams and finishes at 1,211 against 1,481 for the RTX PRO 6000 and 2,045 for the H200, even though the MI350P starts 90 percent ahead of the RTX PRO 6000 at one stream, and the MXFP4 build trails NVFP4 by 41 percent at 128 streams.

The MI350P is the first Instinct card in four years that drops into a standard server, and at 450W in a 2U box it holds up as a PCIe accelerator: 144GB of HBM3E at 4TB/s, 1,120 TFLOPS of FP8 and 2,228 of block-scaled FP4 in MAMF against 820 and 1,634 for the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, and about 2.1x the NVIDIA card’s usable memory bandwidth.

Against the RTX PRO 6000, the MI350P was faster on chat-sized prompts on every FP8, BF16, and GPT-OSS model, by 35 to 65 percent at 128 streams, where HBM3E’s bandwidth and capacity beat a 96GB GDDR7 card, and it leads on both GPT-OSS models at every stream count on both prompt shapes.

The H200 NVL still beat it on the dense FP8 and BF16 tests, by 4 to 18 percent at 128 streams on chat prompts and by more on long prompts, with 20 percent more bandwidth and no FP4 path; on GPT-OSS the MI350P finished 50 and 78 percent ahead of the Hopper card. The larger models are less settled, since four RTX PRO 6000s lead the MI350P pair on GLM-5.2 through 16 streams, with 384GB against 288GB and more aggregate bandwidth and compute to bring to bear.

MiniMax-M3 is closer: the three configurations stay within 10 percent through eight streams on chat prompts, the RTX quad pulls ahead at 16, and the MI350P pair leads on long prompts through eight streams. Per card, the MI350P’s measured FP4 rate is 36 percent higher than the RTX PRO 6000’s, so the advantage is the card count. Those two-card results are on the ROCm 7.2.3 stack and will be run again on ROCm 10.1 alongside the 600W testing.

A definitive opinion on the MI350P is not possible for us yet without testing it at its full potential at 600W, which we plan to do in a PowerEdge XE7745; Dell supports eight MI350Ps at 600W in that chassis. We hear that AMD’s estimate for the extra 150W is about 10 percent more performance.

AMD has come a long way, and the MI350/5X line shows how capable the architecture is. We run an MI300X box in our lab for development, and the pace of the software stack showed in how much of the suite ran on stock vLLM without incident.

With what we saw in this setup, the MI350P is for buyers looking for an alternative to NVIDIA GPUs, either because of lead times, pricing, or to avoid relying on one manufacturer, and Dell’s support for it in the PowerEdge line gives that silicon diversity mainstream servers to fit the need.

To be fair, our work here is far from done. While many buyers may put these cards in 2U servers, there is more performance on the table when they go into a larger chassis designed for 600W cards. However they’re deployed, this is a great first look at AMD returning to the add-in card server market, and as the software stack continues to mature, the MI350P, and what comes next, has a promising future. Today, for a buyer whose models live in the 96GB to 144GB band, the MI350P is one of two PCIe cards that keep them on a single GPU, and the only one past 141GB.
Leaderboard: The AMD Instinct MI350P appears under Also Tested on our Best Enterprise GPUs leaderboard, with its two-card results under Scale-Out Configurations.
