Against the RTX PRO 6000, the MI350P’s memory subsystem is the most immediate difference. It has 50 percent more GPU memory and roughly 2.5x the memory bandwidth. For a model that doesn’t fit comfortably within 96GB, the additional capacity could determine whether it runs on one GPU or needs to be distributed across several.

The RTX PRO 6000, however, serves a broader range of workloads, with hardware for graphics, ray tracing, and video alongside its AI capabilities. The choice weighs more than two peak compute figures; it also depends on what else the system needs to do.

The H200 NVL is the more direct comparison for the MI350P among high-memory PCIe accelerators; the larger Blackwell datacenter GPUs sit in a different class. Memory capacity is nearly identical at 144GB versus the H200’s 141GB, with both using HBM3E, and the H200 offers 20 percent more memory bandwidth at 4.8TB/s. The two also scale differently: all three PCIe cards connect to the host over PCIe, but the H200 NVL adds dedicated GPU-to-GPU connectivity through NVLink bridges connecting up to four GPUs.

The larger MI350X and MI355X were built to compete with Blackwell, but the MI350P cuts that hardware configuration in half. That brings it closer to the H200 NVL in memory attributes and in overall positioning. One place where the MI350P still distinguishes itself is native MXFP4 and MXFP6 support, which matters more as inference moves toward lower precision.

The smaller memory subsystem is another compromise, because AMD has not offset the reduction in HBM stacks with faster HBM3E, leaving the MI350P at 4TB/s of bandwidth and behind the H200 NVL on this metric. That can limit performance in memory-bandwidth-bound workloads, regardless of the available compute, as the memory bandwidth and long-prompt inference results later in the review show.

The DGX Station comparison runs the other way, because the GB300 Station carries a full B300 GPU with one HBM stack disabled, a datacenter-class chip on a datacenter power budget, while the MI350P is half of a datacenter-class chip fitted into the 600W envelope of a PCIe add-in card. AMD needs two or four MI350Ps to meet that single GPU, and on paper two of them do: 288GB and 8TB/s against the Station’s 252GB and 7.1TB/s. Those resources sit on two cards, though, and a workload spanning both exchanges data over PCIe peer-to-peer, which limits how much the second card adds.

The MI350P review unit is a Dell PowerEdge R7725 with two AMD EPYC 9555 processors (64 cores each), 1.5TB of DDR5-6400 across 24 DIMMs, and two MI350P cards set to 450W, the cap for a 2U server. The RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition cards (600W) ran in the Dell PowerEdge XE7740 that carries our four-card inference build, a single H200 NVL (450W) ran in the Dell PowerEdge R770 from our review, and the GB300 figures come from the ASUS ExpertCenter Pro ET900N G3 DGX Station we reviewed in September.

The iDRAC inventory below shows how the two cards are seated. They sit in PCIe slots 2 and 7, both Gen5 x16 and both reporting healthy, and the device keys, 0-139-0 and 1-199-0, read to us as one card behind each EPYC socket, so tensor-parallel traffic between the two MI350Ps crosses the socket link on its way between root complexes. That is the layout a two-card deployment in a 2U server gets by default, and it is worth keeping in mind on the two-card results later.

The memory view shows the rest of the host: 24 DIMMs of 64GB DDR5-6400, dual rank, for 1,536GB in a server that tops out at 6TB, all with multi-bit ECC. The headroom matters for the GLM-5.2 run, where the MXFP4 checkpoint does not fit in two cards’ 288GB and vLLM offloads part of the expert weights to host memory.

To put the MI350P’s compute in context, we ran MAMF across the four systems. MAMF (Maximum Achievable Matmul FLOPS) is a practical performance metric designed to measure the realistic peak floating-point operations per second an accelerator reaches during matrix multiplication, a more useful benchmark than the theoretical peak FLOPS in the spec sheet. We sweep each system in BF16, FP8, and block-scaled FP4 and report the best sustained dense result per precision; the hatched bars multiply each PCIe card’s result by the card count used in the large-model serving runs and are calculated, with no measurement behind them.

At 450W, one MI350P reaches 580 TFLOPS in BF16, 1,120 in FP8, and 2,228 in FP4. The RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell follows at 419, 820, and 1,634, so the MI350P holds a 36 to 38 percent lead over the NVIDIA card at every precision while running 150W below it, with the widest gap in BF16 at 38.4 percent.

The H200 NVL’s 652 TFLOPS in BF16 and 1,205 in FP8 put it ahead of the MI350P on both, and it has no FP4 path. The GB300 DGX Station sits above all three PCIe cards at 1,924, 3,802, and 6,024, roughly 3.3x the MI350P at BF16 and 2.7x at FP4; two MI350Ps on paper close to 1,160 and 4,456, still short of the Station’s single GPU. The NVIDIA MAMF figures in this review come from our latest runs on each card and replace the results from our earlier testing.

Raw compute throughput is only useful if the accelerator can keep its execution units supplied with data. This matters most for inference, where token generation during the decode phase is limited more by memory bandwidth than by available FLOPS. The bandwidth test reads, writes, and copies GPU memory through compute kernels and the copy engine, showing the bandwidth available inside each GPU against its rated figure.

One MI350P reads its HBM3E at 3,291GB/s and writes at 3,204GB/s, about 80 percent of the 4TB/s rating, with copies at 1,276 to 1,283GB/s; a copy consumes bandwidth twice, once to read the source and again to write the destination. The RTX PRO 6000’s GDDR7 manages 1,540GB/s on reads and 1,483GB/s on writes, so the MI350P carries about 2.1x the usable bandwidth per card.

The H200 NVL’s 4,472GB/s read and 4,156GB/s write figures run 36 and 30 percent ahead of the MI350P, in line with its 4.8TB/s rating against 4TB/s, and the GB300 DGX Station reaches 6,869GB/s. Two MI350Ps measured together reach 6,529GB/s on reads, near the Station, but that bandwidth sits in two PCIe slots, and a model spanning both pays for every exchange over PCIe.

With the low-level tests covered, we move to LLM inference. Our vLLM online serving test drives an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with a fixed number of concurrent streams and records output tokens per second across the run. We report two shapes: 512 tokens in and 512 out, which is chat-sized and decode-heavy, and 8,192 in and 1,024 out, which is RAG- and document-sized and leans on prefill. Concurrency doubles from one stream upward, and each chart stops at the highest concurrency at which every card in it completed. Every point is two requests per stream, so single-stream figures rest on two requests and carry more run-to-run variance than the higher-concurrency points.

Each model ran on the fewest cards that could hold it: one MI350P for everything through GPT-OSS-120B and MiniMax-M2.7, and two for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, MiniMax-M3, GLM-5.2, and GLM-5.3 Flash. The RTX PRO 6000 runs follow the same rule, which puts two RTX cards against one MI350P on MiniMax-M2.7 and four against two on MiniMax-M3 and GLM-5.2. Low-precision builds differ by vendor: AMD’s are MXFP4 through Quark, NVIDIA’s are NVFP4, and the FP4 pairings are labeled that way throughout. GPT-OSS ships as MXFP4 and runs the same weights on every card. The H200 NVFP4 builds are not included.

Read down the MI350P column, and the card count is the first thing 144GB gets you. Six of the ten models run on one MI350P, where the RTX PRO 6000’s 96GB needs a second card for MiniMax-M2.7, and the two MXFP4 checkpoints that stay on a pair of MI350Ps, MiniMax-M3 and GLM-5.2, need four RTX PRO 6000s. GLM-5.2 is the one that outgrows even 288GB, and vLLM offloads part of its expert weights to the R7725’s host memory for that run; the GB300 does the same with about 215GB of experts in Grace memory.

The MI350P figures for the single-card models were run October 27 on AMDGPU 31.60, ROCm 10.1.0, and vLLM 0.32.0. Dell’s validated combination is vLLM 0.27 with ROCm 10.0 and AMDGPU 31.5, and we went one step past it to the ROCm 10.1 release of October 5. The NVIDIA cards ran the vLLM 26.08 container on CUDA 13.4.1 throughout. The table lists the build behind each run.

The four two-card models, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, MiniMax-M3, GLM-5.2, and GLM-5.3 Flash, are reported from runs on ROCm 7.2.3. Our ROCm 10.1 passes on those models used CPU expert offload throughout and, on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, a speculative decoder the NVIDIA runs did not, which makes them a different test, so they are held for a clean pass on the current stack, and the tables label every MI350P row with its stack.

AMD’s preferred path for these models is its AIM containers; the Enterprise AI Suite 2.5 release of October 9 is validated on ROCm 10 and carries AIMs for GPT-OSS-120B, Llama 3.3 70B, and Gemma 3 27B, but AMD’s accelerator table lists an optimized MI350P profile only for Wan2.2 so far. Stock vLLM is therefore still the path an MI350P buyer takes today, and is what we measured.

There are 28 charts below, so here is the short version in two tables: output tokens per second for each model at the highest concurrency every card completed, with the chat-sized 512-in, 512-out workload first. The MI350P figures are one card at 450W unless the row says otherwise, with a column for the stack each row comes from; the GB300 DGX Station is a single B300.

Two results stand out in the chat table: the MI350P beats the RTX PRO 6000 on every FP8, BF16, and GPT-OSS model, by 35 to 65 percent at 128 streams, trails NVIDIA’s NVFP4 builds only at the top of the Llama and MiniMax-M2.7 curves, and roughly doubles the NVIDIA card at a single stream on Llama 3.1 8B and Mistral Small 24B, where 4TB/s of HBM3E does the work.

The H200 NVL, with 20 percent more bandwidth, stays 4 to 18 percent ahead on the dense FP8 and BF16 models at 128 streams and ties on Llama 3.1 8B FP8; on the two GPT-OSS models the order reverses, and the MI350P finishes 50 and 78 percent ahead.
The second table repeats the exercise on the 8,192-token prompts, where prefill dominates the run and the balance between compute and memory bandwidth shifts toward the NVIDIA cards.

On prefill-heavy prompts, the picture is mixed: the MI350P leads the RTX PRO 6000 on both GPT-OSS models at every stream count and on Mistral Small, splits Qwen3-Coder at 128 streams (24 percent ahead on BF16, 8 percent behind on FP8), and flattens by 16 streams on Llama and MiniMax-M2.7, where it finishes behind the NVIDIA card. Against the H200, it leads on GPT-OSS by 15 percent on the 120B model and 5 percent on the 20B at 128 streams and trails by 25 to 58 percent on the dense models.

On the largest models, where two MI350Ps face four RTX PRO 6000s, the NVIDIA set leads GLM-5.2 through 16 streams on the chat workload with 384GB of GDDR7 against 288GB of HBM3E, while on MiniMax-M3 all three configurations stay within 10 percent through eight streams before the RTX quad pulls ahead at 16. The single GB300 clears every PCIe configuration by a wide margin on anything that fits in its 252GB.

GLM-5.3 Flash was not run on the RTX PRO 6000, so the comparison is two MI350P cards against the single GB300 Station through 32 streams. On the chat workload, the MI350P pair starts behind, 45 against 353 output tokens per second at one stream, and crosses the Station at eight streams on its way to 1,462 at 32, against 828 for the Station. On the prefill-heavy workload the Station leads throughout, 1,219 against 760 at 32 streams, where the pair’s prefill has to cross PCIe between the two cards and the B300 does it all in one piece of HBM.

GLM-5.2 is the memory story in this set. The MXFP4 checkpoint spills past the two MI350P cards’ 288GB into host memory, so single-stream throughput is 2 output tokens per second on the pair against 9 for four RTX PRO 6000 cards holding the NVFP4 build in 384GB of GDDR7 and 35 for the Station, which offloads about 215GB of expert weights to Grace memory. The RTX quad leads through 16 streams on the chat workload; at 32 the MI350P pair reaches 59 against 40, and the Station reaches 139. On prefill-heavy prompts, neither PCIe configuration gets past single digits through 16 streams, against 87 for the Station.

Two MI350Ps hold the MXFP4 build of MiniMax-M3 in 288GB; the NVIDIA side needs four RTX PRO 6000 cards. The three configurations run within 10 percent of each other through eight streams on the chat workload; the RTX quad pulls ahead at 16 (1,181 against 998 for the pair and 940 for the Station), and at 32 the MI350P pair reads 1,509 against 759 for the quad and 1,041 for the Station.

On prefill-heavy prompts, the MI350P pair leads at every point through eight streams, 524 against 444 for the quad, while the Station, which keeps a slice of this model’s experts in Grace memory, falls to 103.

With two cards on each side and the native FP8 checkpoint, the RTX PRO 6000 pair leads through eight streams on the chat workload and the MI350P pair takes over from 16, finishing at 1,081 against 829 at 32 streams; the single Station reaches 1,766 at the same point. The prefill-heavy run follows the same shape, the MI350P pair at 621 against 345 for the RTX pair at 32 streams and 954 for the Station.

One MI350P carries the MXFP4 build of MiniMax-M2.7 against two RTX PRO 6000 cards on NVFP4. The single MI350P leads the pair at one stream (124 against 115), stays 8 to 20 percent ahead through 64 streams 1,486 against 1,339, then flattens at 1,524 at 128 and 1,557 at 256, while the RTX pair continues to 1,932 and 2,842; the Station reaches 4,793.
On the prefill-heavy workload, the MI350P holds at 304 to 331 output tokens per second from eight streams through 64, against 501 for the RTX pair and 1,744 for the Station.

GPT-OSS ships as MXFP4, so every card runs the same weights. One MI350P leads one RTX PRO 6000 at every stream count on both workloads, by 40 to 93 percent from four streams up, and finishes at 5,057 output tokens per second on the chat workload and 2,101 on prefill-heavy prompts at 128 streams, against 3,064 and 1,169 for the RTX PRO 6000 and 3,376 and 1,825 for the H200 NVL; the Station reaches 9,280 and 5,023.

AMD and Dell’s MLPerf Inference v6.1 submission of September 16 puts a ceiling on the same model: eight MI350Ps in a PowerEdge XE7745 produced 48,971 tokens per second offline and 40,868 in the server scenario on GPT-OSS-120B, which is 6,121 and 5,108 per GPU, on a tuned submission stack. That harness and ours are not like-for-like, but the 5,057 we measured at 128 streams on stock vLLM sits at the bottom of that range.

The smaller OpenAI model follows the same curve. The MI350P leads the RTX PRO 6000 at every point, 8,174 against 4,992 at 64 streams and 10,726 against 7,937 at 128 on the chat workload, and 3,460 against 2,083 and 3,603 against 2,482 on prefill-heavy prompts, and it runs to 16,406 at 256 streams where the RTX PRO 6000 reads 11,077. The H200 NVL trails the MI350P on both shapes, at 6,022 and 3,419 at 128 streams, and the Station sits at 22,041 and 9,555.

The 30B MoE with 3B active parameters gives the MI350P a lead over the RTX PRO 6000 at every concurrency on the chat workload, finishing at 6,451 against 3,995 on FP8 and 4,696 against 2,881 on BF16 at 128 streams, with the H200 at 7,459 and 5,240.

On prefill-heavy prompts, the FP8 run leads only through four streams and then trails the RTX PRO 6000 from eight through 128, 759 against 823 at the top, with the H200 at 1,820; the BF16 run climbs to 728 at 128 streams against 588 and 1,592.

Mistral Small is the MI350P’s strongest dense result against the RTX PRO 6000: 4,458 against 3,242 on FP8 and 3,065 against 2,026 on BF16 at 128 streams on the chat workload, and at one stream the MI350P roughly doubles the NVIDIA card (100 against 56 on FP8, 67 against 32 on BF16).

It is also the dense model where the MI350P leads on prefill-heavy prompts, 599 against 482 on FP8 at 128 streams and 425 against 299 on BF16 at 64, though the H200 reaches 799 and 632 at the same points.

Llama 3.1 8B is here for continuity with our older GPU coverage. At 128 streams on the chat workload, the MI350P delivers 11,045 output tokens per second on FP8 against 8,073 for the RTX PRO 6000 and 11,054 for the H200, a tie with the Hopper card, and 6,819 on BF16 against 4,740 and 8,069. AMD’s MXFP4 build reaches 8,383 at 128 streams, 5 percent behind NVIDIA’s NVFP4 build on the RTX PRO 6000 (8,869), after leading it by 12 to 143 percent at every lower stream count; at a single stream the MXFP4 run reads 323 against 133.

The prefill-heavy runs invert the result: MI350P FP8 flattens by 16 streams and finishes at 1,211 against 1,481 for the RTX PRO 6000 and 2,045 for the H200, even though the MI350P starts 90 percent ahead of the RTX PRO 6000 at one stream, and the MXFP4 build trails NVFP4 by 41 percent at 128 streams.

The MI350P is the first Instinct card in four years that drops into a standard server, and at 450W in a 2U box it holds up as a PCIe accelerator: 144GB of HBM3E at 4TB/s, 1,120 TFLOPS of FP8 and 2,228 of block-scaled FP4 in MAMF against 820 and 1,634 for the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, and about 2.1x the NVIDIA card’s usable memory bandwidth.

Against the RTX PRO 6000, the MI350P was faster on chat-sized prompts on every FP8, BF16, and GPT-OSS model, by 35 to 65 percent at 128 streams, where HBM3E’s bandwidth and capacity beat a 96GB GDDR7 card, and it leads on both GPT-OSS models at every stream count on both prompt shapes.

The H200 NVL still beat it on the dense FP8 and BF16 tests, by 4 to 18 percent at 128 streams on chat prompts and by more on long prompts, with 20 percent more bandwidth and no FP4 path; on GPT-OSS the MI350P finished 50 and 78 percent ahead of the Hopper card. The larger models are less settled, since four RTX PRO 6000s lead the MI350P pair on GLM-5.2 through 16 streams, with 384GB against 288GB and more aggregate bandwidth and compute to bring to bear.

MiniMax-M3 is closer: the three configurations stay within 10 percent through eight streams on chat prompts, the RTX quad pulls ahead at 16, and the MI350P pair leads on long prompts through eight streams. Per card, the MI350P’s measured FP4 rate is 36 percent higher than the RTX PRO 6000’s, so the advantage is the card count. Those two-card results are on the ROCm 7.2.3 stack and will be run again on ROCm 10.1 alongside the 600W testing.

A definitive opinion on the MI350P is not possible for us yet without testing it at its full potential at 600W, which we plan to do in a PowerEdge XE7745; Dell supports eight MI350Ps at 600W in that chassis. We hear that AMD’s estimate for the extra 150W is about 10 percent more performance.

AMD has come a long way, and the MI350/5X line shows how capable the architecture is. We run an MI300X box in our lab for development, and the pace of the software stack showed in how much of the suite ran on stock vLLM without incident.

With what we saw in this setup, the MI350P is for buyers looking for an alternative to NVIDIA GPUs, either because of lead times, pricing, or to avoid relying on one manufacturer, and Dell’s support for it in the PowerEdge line gives that silicon diversity mainstream servers to fit the need.

To be fair, our work here is far from done. While many buyers may put these cards in 2U servers, there is more performance on the table when they go into a larger chassis designed for 600W cards. However they’re deployed, this is a great first look at AMD returning to the add-in card server market, and as the software stack continues to mature, the MI350P, and what comes next, has a promising future. Today, for a buyer whose models live in the 96GB to 144GB band, the MI350P is one of two PCIe cards that keep them on a single GPU, and the only one past 141GB.

rssBodyEvidence: Intel has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Classiq, a quantum computing software company based in Tel Aviv, and plans to pair Classiq’s algorithm synthesis platform with its silicon spin-qubit hardware to sell a full quantum stack. Intel did not disclose the price. The deal needs regulatory approval and is expected to close in the first half of 2027, and the two companies operate independently until then.

Classiq’s platform combines AI agents, a high-level quantum modeling language, and design automation to turn a problem description into optimized, hardware-ready quantum circuits, and it runs those circuits across quantum hardware from multiple vendors. Intel compares the role to what electronic design automation (EDA) and computer-aided design (CAD) tools did for chip design: a common software layer that hides the hardware underneath so developers do not hand-build gate-level circuits. Classiq says dozens of global enterprises use the platform, which also handles hardware benchmarking and cost and performance optimization.

Intel says it will keep supporting Classiq’s existing integrations with other vendors’ quantum hardware after the deal closes, and that the software will stay agnostic to qubit modality and hardware. That matters because Classiq’s customers run on other vendors’ quantum hardware today, none of it built on Intel’s silicon.

Intel has worked on quantum computing since 2015 and builds spin qubits in silicon on the same kind of equipment and processes it uses for conventional chips. The company says it is the only one able to produce qubit chips and the cryogenic control electronics that go with them at scale that way. Adding Classiq’s software would make Intel a full-stack quantum provider and put quantum processing units (QPUs) next to the CPUs, GPUs, and ASICs it already sells.

“For more than a decade, Intel has made remarkable progress in quantum computing by applying its semiconductor innovation, advanced manufacturing prowess and systems engineering expertise to the development of scalable silicon spin-qubit technology,” said Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive officer, Intel. “Joining forces with Classiq transforms Intel’s Quantum Computing Group into a full-stack quantum computing business.”

Nir Minerbi, Classiq’s co-founder and chief executive officer, said the company has focused since its founding on letting developers, researchers, and enterprises build scalable quantum applications without deep expertise in circuit design. The move puts Intel on a different path from IBM , which builds its stack around superconducting qubits, and from the trapped-ion and neutral-atom vendors.

rssBodyEvidence: Cadence has introduced the Maestro AI Model Portfolio, a set of domain-specialized models that power its AI Super Agents across chip and system design. Maestro combines post-trained large language models, trained decision models, and self-improving agent skills, and Cadence says initial design-workflow results show up to 30 percent higher quality of results and up to 5X better token efficiency than a general-purpose foundation model. These are vendor results, and we did not run or audit them.

Cadence credits those gains to a vertically integrated learning environment that ties the Maestro models to its AI Super Agents, its electronic design automation (EDA) and system design automation (SDA) tools, curated engineering datasets, and evaluation harnesses. Cadence’s deterministic solvers score agent output against engineering objectives, constraints, and ground truth, which gives reinforcement learning a closed, verified feedback loop. Cadence has not published the workloads or baselines behind the 30 percent and 5X figures.

Super Agents use Maestro alongside general models: given a high-level objective, a Super Agent interprets the design intent, breaks it into tasks, routes work among Maestro, frontier, and open-weight models, and drives the EDA and SDA tools. Cadence says balancing tool calls against model invocations is what reduces token use. Customers can also post-train Maestro models, including NVIDIA Nemotron variants, on proprietary data, designs, and workflows.

NVIDIA contributes Nemotron models, OpenShell , and engineering expertise, and the two companies are integrating Cadence’s agents with the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for agent security. “By grounding reinforcement learning in feedback from EDA tools and deterministic solvers, we can teach agents to make better design decisions based on how well their work meets engineering objectives and constraints,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA.

Maestro serves four Super Agents named in the announcement, each mapped to a stage of the design flow. ChipStack handles front-end digital design and verification, from RTL generation and testbench creation through regression and debug. ViraStack covers custom and analog design, InnoStack takes digital implementation, signoff, and 3D-IC, and AuraStack targets PCB and advanced packaging. rssBodyEvidence: CloudCasa by Catalogic has added Dell PowerStore to the storage arrays CloudCasa Disaster Recovery can drive for Kubernetes failover, alongside HPE Alletra and SUSE Storage. The same feature update adds a read-only Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets AI assistants check backup and DR status, and a preview of Changed Block Tracking (CBT) for KubeVirt virtual machine backups, which copies only the blocks that changed since the last run.

PowerStore joins the HPE Alletra Storage MP B10000 , HPE Alletra 9000, and SUSE Storage as replication providers for CloudCasa DR. The division of labor is the same on each platform: the array replicates persistent volume data to the recovery site, synchronously or asynchronously in PowerStore’s case, and CloudCasa handles the Kubernetes side of failover and failback for containerized applications and KubeVirt VMs. Volume data moves array to array and never passes through CloudCasa.

CloudCasa records the configuration of each protected workload in a replicated inventory volume and talks to the array through the PowerStore REST API. On failover, it brings up that inventory volume first, starts a recovery agent on the target cluster, then fails over the remaining PowerStore volume groups and rebuilds the Deployments, StatefulSets, persistent volume claims, and KubeVirt VMs against the replicated volumes. Because PowerStore fails over complete volume groups, CloudCasa advises placing workloads with different recovery requirements in separate groups.

Failback waits for operator confirmation, after which CloudCasa reverses replication on the affected volume groups so PowerStore resynchronizes only the changes made since the failover, scales down the workloads still running at the DR site, and then fails the volume groups back to the primary array and rebuilds the workloads there. CloudCasa says the approach targets recovery times measured in minutes and near-zero RPO when PowerStore replicates synchronously, with results depending on replication mode, workload size, and distance between sites.

The integration covers block (SCSI) persistent volumes provisioned through the PowerStore CSI driver; NFS and SMB volume DR is on CloudCasa’s roadmap. Supported platforms include Red Hat OpenShift and OpenShift Virtualization, SUSE Rancher/RKE2 and SUSE Virtualization, VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, and upstream Kubernetes 1.20 and later. CloudCasa DR is licensed per worker node on an annual subscription, separately from CloudCasa’s backup product, in both the SaaS and self-hosted editions.

The MCP server lets any AI assistant that supports remote MCP servers over HTTP query CloudCasa in plain language, with questions such as which backup jobs failed in the last 24 hours or which recovery points exist for a namespace. It calls the CloudCasa APIs on the user’s behalf, authenticates with a CloudCasa API key passed in an HTTP header, and can do only what that key’s role allows. For now it is read-only: assistants can list clusters, backup policies, jobs, recovery points, restores, alerts, and backup targets, but cannot run, create, edit, or delete anything.

“Platform teams do more of their day-to-day work using AI assistants, and they want backup status available alongside the rest of their tooling,” said Ryan Kaw, Global VP of Sales and Alliances at CloudCasa. “The MCP server makes that possible today.”

The CBT preview builds on the incremental backup support KubeVirt added in version 1.8, which uses QEMU and libvirt backup capabilities and works regardless of the underlying storage. CBT records which disk blocks changed since the previous backup, so CloudCasa copies only those blocks, which the company says shortens VM backup times. On Red Hat OpenShift, that KubeVirt version arrives with OpenShift 4.22, and the feature has to be enabled explicitly.

The PowerStore DR integration and the MCP server are available now, and CBT backups remain in preview. The update also adds a dedicated VMs page that lists virtual machines across all registered clusters with their running state and guest agent status, where admins can define backups and restores for each VM.

rssBodyEvidence: Cigent Software Full Drive Encryption and its command line interface have received Intel vPro Certified App status, Intel’s validation that a background application meets its power and performance targets on vPro business PCs. Cigent’s software is a CSfC-listed encryption component used in NSA Commercial Solutions for Classified data-at-rest architectures, so the certification speaks to a specific buyer: defense and government IT teams running encrypted laptops and field systems where battery life and processor headroom are part of the mission.

Intel’s program evaluates software that runs continuously in the background, such as security, telemetry, and observability agents, for CPU utilization, power efficiency, coordination of background threads, use of the hybrid core architecture, and the number of CPU interruptions it generates. Intel says Cigent’s software met or exceeded those targets in its testing with minimal impact on device performance and battery life, though neither company has published the measured figures. Cigent joins a certified list that includes CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Citrix Workspace, and Absolute Secure Endpoint.

Cigent Software Full Drive Encryption is the independent inner encryption layer in the NSA CSfC Data at Rest Capability Package v5.1.0 architecture. It runs once the outer hardware encryption layer has authenticated, with separate credentials and key management and optional smart card authentication that requires both the card and its PIN. Cigent uses AES-256 and positions the software for National Security Systems spanning endpoints, servers, tactical edge systems, vehicles, and autonomous platforms, with Dell, Getac, and Panasonic PCs, mobile workstations, and servers among the supported hardware.

“For defense teams operating mobile platforms in the field, every hour of battery life counts, and so does every ounce of performance. Earning Intel vPro Certified App status for Cigent Software Full Drive Encryption and CLI reflects our commitment to minimizing our software’s power use and processor demands. That efficiency supports CSfC Data-at-Rest deployments on the Intel vPro devices those teams depend on,” said Juan Mojica, Chief Technology Officer at Cigent.

“Cigent’s Intel vPro Certified App status reflects a critical priority on efficiency and optimization that can help customers confidently deploy security technologies across their PC fleets,” said Dennis Luo, Senior Director and General Manager, Worldwide AI PC Developer Relations at Intel.

The CLI covers deployment and management for organizations running the software at scale, and the certification applies to it as well as to the encryption software. Cigent says the encryption can be rolled out across large fleets with standard enterprise software-distribution tools, using MSI installation flags to preconfigure passwords, define authorized users, and enable self-enrollment without a separate management console. Neither company has published the test configurations, the vPro generations covered, or the CPU and power figures behind the certification, and Cigent has not tied pricing or availability changes to it.

rssBodyEvidence: The biggest AI infrastructure decision many enterprises make in the next year won’t be a GPU investment; it will be a database upgrade. Oracle AI Database 26ai is the long-term support release Oracle is steering its 19c installed base toward. 26ai puts vector search in the same engine that holds transactions. When the vector index lives in the database, the block array and the SAN fabric behind it become AI infrastructure, carrying retrieval traffic alongside the transactions they already serve.

Oracle built 26ai around that idea: a native VECTOR data type, SQL vector search functions, in-database model execution through ONNX, and SELECT AI for natural language queries, all in an LTS release the company enumerates at more than 300 new features. In practice, a DBA can generate embeddings, store them next to the rows they describe, and run a similarity search within the same transaction scope as an order lookup. There’s no separate vector store to run, no synchronization pipeline to maintain, and no second copy of regulated data living outside the audit trail.

IBM cites IDC on the trend: “Integrated vector databases are the clear platform of choice for storing and querying vector embeddings, as organizations favor unified, governed environments for agentic AI.” IBM and Broadcom’s customers want to extend the database they already trust before standing up a new one alongside it. Oracle is not alone in this direction. DB-Engines’ October 2026 popularity ranking lists the top four relational and multi-model engines: Oracle, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, and PostgreSQL, and all four have added vector types or vector search, natively or through extensions such as pgvector. IBM chose to start its validation work with Oracle primarily because of its market leadership, though the storage argument in this piece applies to the others as well.

The arguments for keeping block storage on-prem haven’t changed with AI in the picture: the data that makes an AI deployment useful, such as patient records, claims, orders, and trades, can’t leave. Copying it to a dedicated AI platform means paying for storage twice, accepting that the copy drifts from the production cluster, and losing the governance controls that made the original legally defensible. Keeping retrieval inside the database avoids all three. The array that serves a sub-millisecond row lookup now also serves a vector similarity scan for a clinician and a backup stream at the same time.

IBM Storage and Broadcom’s Fibre Channel (FC) group set out to validate that mixed-workload case, and built an environment around Oracle AI Database 26ai on IBM FlashSystem with Broadcom’s Brocade Gen 8 SAN fabric and Emulex 64G SecureHBAs . They then worked through the questions an infrastructure team had been asking: what is the impact on transactional latency when a vector workload starts next to it, the effect of fabric speed on vector search throughput, the capacity consumed by embeddings, the effectiveness of ransomware detection when targeting an RMAN backup volume, and what are the requirements for adding a host to the SAN without a zoning ticket?

None of this says AI workloads in general belong on block storage. Enterprises will keep file and object arrays for the unstructured estate: documents, images, video, training sets, and model checkpoints that never lived in a database and likely never will. In the healthcare demonstration that follows, IBM keeps the raw X-ray images in object storage while storing only the embeddings and case metadata in Oracle. What changes is the burden on the array, which now carries several workloads with very different I/O profiles at the same time.

The relational tier is the most familiar one: millions of random 4KB to 16KB I/Os per second, row lookups and commits that need to land in microseconds, heavy write concurrency from redo, undo, and checkpoint traffic, and a tail latency that stays predictable because a user-facing application is waiting on it. RMAN, Oracle’s backup utility, is the opposite: a sequential stream that needs headroom to finish inside its window without disturbing the first workload. Both are well understood, and IBM’s arrays are tuned for them.

The vector tier is harder to characterize because large tables of vector embeddings can make vector search look like a bandwidth-intensive workload: a large sequential scan. IBM’s characterization of the Oracle 26ai vector path is closer to OLTP. Each hop through the index is a roughly 4KB random read; the query path is IOPS-bound and latency-sensitive, and reads dominate because writes live in a separate ingest and index-build phase.

Bandwidth matters in bursts, when an index is built or a corpus is re-embedded, and those bursts tend to be quite large. That split is the core of the mixed-I/O problem: on the query path, the vector workload competes with transactions for the same queues, making isolation a quality-of-service concern. And the bursty phases are where fabric bandwidth becomes the ceiling, as the 32G versus 64G results later in this piece show.

IBM and Broadcom built one environment for this validation in Broadcom’s Colorado AI lab. The storage is an IBM FlashSystem 9000 series array running IBM Storage Virtualize 9.1.3 with 24 FlashCore Modules, presenting 64G Fibre Channel ports to a pair of Brocade Gen 8 G820 SAN switches. The database host is a dual-socket Intel Xeon 6767P server with two 2-port Emulex LPe38102 64G SecureHBAs, running Oracle AI Database 26ai on ASM with no GPU in the storage path; IBM Storage Insights watches the array.

We ran the fabric and capacity results, the 32G versus 64G vector search comparison, and the footprint measurements using VectorDBBench against the BioASQ 1M dataset on that host alone. The same configuration also supports the application workload. A Supermicro 821GE-TNHR with two Xeon Platinum 8470 processors and eight NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs hosts the healthcare application and its language model. The software stack includes Oracle’s in-database ONNX embedding, Ollama serving Llama 3, and NVIDIA cuVS. A Broadcom Tomahawk 5 switch and Thor 2 400GbE NICs connect the two servers. The I/O QoS, multi-tenancy, ransomware detection, and healthcare demonstrations ran in this environment.

According to IBM, the FlashSystem family (the 5300 and 5600, 7300 and 7600, and 9500 and 9600) runs the same Storage Virtualize software, and the functions demonstrated here, including I/O throttling, AutoZoning, ransomware detection, Policy-Based HA, and storage partition migration, work the same way with Oracle AI Database 26ai on any of those arrays at the same code level. Performance and density vary by model and FlashCore Module generation, so every figure in this piece belongs to the system it was measured on.

The first question IBM and Broadcom set out to answer is the one every DBA asks when a vector workload is proposed for the production array: what happens to the core transactions? IBM ran it as two demonstrations on the FlashSystem 9000 series array using volume-level I/O throttles, the mechanism behind what IBM calls I/O QoS. The database was laid out across 30 volumes: 15 for the OLTP tablespaces (ORCL16 through ORCL30) under Swingbench Order Entry at 192 users, and 15 for the vector tables (ORCL31 through ORCL45) under a 200-thread synthetic generator running top-k 500 similarity queries, with Storage Insights charting each volume group.

With OLTP running alone, each OLTP volume held a flat 20,500 ops/s. When the vector generator started, the vector volumes climbed to about 73,000 ops/s each within a minute, and the OLTP volumes fell to about 13,000, a 37 percent drop with nothing changed on the transactional side. The vector search path is 4KB random reads at the same block size as the transactions, so it hits the same queues and takes whatever the array will give it.

A 45,000 IOPS cap on each vector volume, one line of mkthrottle at the CLI, pulled the vector volumes to the limit and lifted OLTP back to about 17,000 ops/s. Removing the cap reversed it, and when the vector run ended, OLTP returned to 20,500. The dashboard tracked the same thing in aggregate: 1.28 million IOPS unthrottled and roughly 950,000 under the cap, which, within a few percent, is the per-volume rate times 30 volumes.

The second demo is the configuration IBM expects would deploy in production: caps set first, 45,000 IOPS per vector volume and 20,000 per OLTP volume, then both workloads launched together. The vector volumes ran at their ceiling, the OLTP volumes settled at about 12,200 ops/s and stayed flat for the length of the run, and the array held 870,000 IOPS (800,000 read, 70,000 write) at 377 microseconds and 6.9GB/s on 25% CPU. The OLTP cap sat above the workload’s demand and never engaged; it’s there so a runaway on either side can’t starve the other.

Swingbench held its 192 users at about 1.19 million transactions per minute, roughly 19,500 TPS, for the length of the run. The generator was tuned to saturate its volumes, so its per-query latency isn’t an application benchmark. Over the 30-minute run, it completed 35,672 queries at 19.8 per second, with a median latency of about 10 seconds and a p99 of 14.3 seconds against a 15-second application timeout; 99 queries (0.28 percent) hit that timeout, and the transactions never noticed any of it.

A FlashSystem throttle is a volume ceiling enforced at the array regardless of host or path, with an optional bandwidth limit alongside the IOPS limit; it caps the neighbor and reserves nothing. The cap is a sizing exercise: 15 vector volumes at 45,000 IOPS is 675,000 IOPS of vector headroom, which left this array’s OLTP volumes what they needed. A different array or mix moves the number around some. Set the vector cap where the transactions hold their latency, and the vector workload gets everything above it.

Sophos’s 2024 survey of 2,974 organizations hit by ransomware found that 94 percent saw the attackers go after their backups, that the attempt succeeded 57 percent of the time, and that median recovery costs ran eight times higher when it did. IBM built the test on the same premise, backups first and production second, and aimed the attack at the RMAN backup target while leaving the database volumes alone. RMAN wrote its backup sets to FlashSystem volumes, a ransomware simulator was run against them, and the array was left to notice on its own, with no host agent in the path.

Detection happens inside the drives: FCM4 and FCM5 FlashCore Modules compute entropy and compressibility on every write as it lands, along with block size, address, and rewrite patterns, and every two seconds pass a per-volume summary to an inference engine inside Storage Virtualize (8.6.3 or later with FCM firmware 4.1 or later). The model raises alerts in the FlashSystem GUI and IBM Storage Insights Pro, forwards them to Storage Defender or a SIEM, and is patchable on its own, so a retrained model ships as a small security update with no firmware upgrade.

Because the analysis runs on the module, it keeps working even when the host is what’s compromised. Encrypted output is high-entropy and stops compressing, and that shows up in the statistics whether the attacker changes file extensions, encrypts only every other block, or slows the rate to hide from an endpoint agent.

During validation, RMAN wrote the backup over 16 parallel channels, with each backup set capped at 150GB, and the database sat on 15 x 200GB disks per ASM disk group for OLTP and vector data. IBM ran the attack against that backup target, and the alert reached Storage Insights in under 60 seconds, which is within the detection window IBM publishes for the feature. Storage Insights flagged all 31 volumes in the volume group, since an alert on one volume marks the whole group as a threat. The response is Safeguarded Copy, and the array handled it without an operator: the FlashSystem took an immutable snapshot of the affected volume group the moment the threat was raised and extended the retention of the last-known good snapshot at the same time. The lsanomalydetection output from the array shows the configuration behind that: inference engine 8.0 with model 0.3.42.0, anomaly_snapshot on, 30 days of retention on the new snapshot, and 30 days added to the last good one. Storage Virtualize also marks the suspect snapshot so nobody restores from it, leaving a clean restore point from before the encryption began.

The fabric also carries a security layer. Broadcom builds post-quantum cryptography into Brocade Gen 8 platforms, the Emulex SecureHBAs encrypt data in flight from host to storage array across that fabric, and FCIA’s new FC-SP-3 standard sets the quantum-ready security baseline for Fibre Channel as a whole.

Adding a host to a Fibre Channel SAN usually takes a ticket and two teams: the server admin collects the HBA WWPNs, the SAN admin builds zones on both fabrics by hand, and the storage admin maps the host to the right target ports. One mistyped WWPN leaves a new Oracle RAC node without its paths. AutoZoning moves that work to the array: FlashSystem talks to the fabric directly, identifies the initiator WWPNs, selects target ports, and creates the zones itself, with no one logging into a switch.

The feature is built on Brocade Target Driven Zoning (TDZ) and arrived in FlashSystem software 9.1.2. It requires Brocade switches running Fabric OS 9.1.1 or later, with TDZ enabled by the fabric administrator on the switch ports facing FlashSystem target ports. That enablement is the one step that stays with the SAN team, and AutoZoning takes no action on a port until it’s done. From there, FlashSystem builds peer zones, allowing host initiators to reach the target port but not each other, under a predictable IBM_SV_ name that marks them as array-managed.

Setup starts in the Fibre Channel port view, which now shows the switch each port connects to, whether the port is AutoZone capable, and whether its connectivity is symmetric, meaning the same port ID on every node lands on the same fabric. A topology view maps that in color, and only green ports that are active, AutoZone capable, and symmetric support AutoZoning. Asymmetric ports stay out even if otherwise capable, since the GUI warns it can compromise redundancy and failover.

Host creation starts from an Unconfigured hosts list, filled through FDMI, which reports each HBA’s host name, operating system, and ports to the fabric. In IBM’s walkthrough, the Add Host dialog opened with the server name, operating system, and both HBA ports of a host that had no zones yet already populated; the admin picked an AutoZone-enabled port set, which defines the target ports the host can reach, and clicked Add. FlashSystem paired its target ports with the host initiators, pushed the zones to both switches, and the host came online with four paths across two fabrics.

For Oracle, IBM positions AutoZoning for adding RAC nodes and replacing HBAs, since the feature tracks changes in host or storage connectivity and adapts zone definitions to match, so a swapped HBA doesn’t require a manual rezone. The same automation applies when hosts need paths to a second array for storage partition migration or Policy-Based HA (PBHA). The SAN team still controls which target ports participate, since nothing happens on a port until they enable TDZ. Consequently, adding a host no longer waits on a zoning change.

Policy-Based HA (PBHA) synchronously replicates a storage partition between two FlashSystem arrays at metro distance, with active-active host access at both sites. IBM says the feature is designed for zero RPO and for a storage failover that a properly clustered Oracle deployment can ride through without data loss. When the failed site comes back, the data resyncs and the workload moves back without an outage.

The FlashSystem Grid feature federates up to 32 FlashSystem arrays under one management view, and storage partition migration moves a partition, with its volumes, volume groups, and hosts, from one array to another without application downtime. For Oracle, IBM points to hardware refresh, draining a system before a firmware update, and moving a vector partition to a system with more capacity as the embedding set grows. A system migrates one partition at a time over Fibre Channel or high-speed Ethernet; hosts can connect over Fibre Channel, iSCSI, or NVMe/TCP, and a partition already configured for PBHA is not eligible for migration.

The Storage Insights placement advisor handles planning for the same grid. Given a workload’s capacity, growth rate, I/O profile, and latency target, it scores every system in the grid, ranks the best fit before anything is provisioned, and can also recommend a migration when it spots a CPU or IOPS imbalance. Migration and placement both use Storage Insights Pro, with every grid system registered to the same Storage Insights tenant.

Multi-tenancy lets a DBA team and an AI team share that grid without sharing administration. In IBM’s walkthrough, an administrator created two tenants on the same array (Tenant_Scale and Tenant_oracle_ai) and gave each one a system, a user group with a tenant role, and a first user. They then built a storage partition for each with a separate volume group, volumes, and host mappings. The GUI offers to configure replication as soon as a new partition exists. Logged in as the Tenant_Scale user, the GUI showed only that tenant’s partition and resources, with nothing belonging to Tenant_oracle_ai, and the same check from the Tenant_oracle_ai side returned the same result.

The one variable IBM and Broadcom changed in this testing, on purpose, was the fabric. The same array, host, and Emulex LPe38102 SecureHBAs ran VectorDBBench against the BioASQ 1M dataset (one million 1,024-dimension vectors from the biomedical question-answering corpus) twice: once with the two HBA ports at 32G and once at 64G, through the same Brocade G820 switches. Everything else, from the 16 ASM volumes to the 4GB SGA, stayed put, so the difference between the two runs is the Fibre Channel generation and nothing else.

The search phase of this benchmark is a read-only scan: Oracle’s IVF_FLAT index routes each query to a cluster of partitions and reads them in full, and with 1,024-dimension FLOAT32 vectors, that is a bandwidth workload. On two 32G ports, host-side reads leveled at 6.3GB/s, the line rate of the pair, and the search curve flattened at 43.7 queries per second with 20 threads. On two 64G ports, the same host read at 12.5GB/s and kept scaling to 85.0 QPS at 80 threads, 95% more throughput from the same storage.

Latency tells the other part of the 64G story: at one thread the two fabrics are within 8% of each other, 0.107 seconds against 0.099, because a single query never fills either pipe. From five threads on, however, the 32G run queues: average latency doubles the 64G figure at every step, and at 80 threads p99 reaches 4.08 seconds against 1.14. A saturated FC fabric doesn’t fail; it queues every query, and that wait shows up as tail latency.

The load phase moved too; ingesting the million vectors took 94.1 seconds on 32G and 84.5 on 64G, and the IVF_FLAT index build took 139.6 seconds against 108.4, 28.8% longer on the slower fabric, for a total load of 233.7 seconds against 193.0. Recall and NDCG were within 0.1% across the two runs (83.81% and 84.42% on 32G, 83.95% and 84.56% on 64G), so the fabric changed how quickly answers arrived. For a database that has been on 32G since deployment, the HBA and switch upgrade is an obvious opportunity to deliver more performance.

Vector search changes the capacity math before it changes performance. An embedding is a fixed-width numeric copy of a chunk of source data, and for text that copy is usually larger than the chunk it describes: a 1,000-byte passage becomes a 1,024-dimension FLOAT32 vector of 4,096 bytes before the database adds a row to hold it. The team calls this vector storage amplification, and measured it on the same BioASQ 1M dataset used in the fabric comparison.

The source text behind the million vectors is 0.90GB. In Oracle 26ai, it became a 7.67GB vector table, including about 0.3GB of row overhead, and the IVF_FLAT index added 8.57GB on top because it keeps a second, clustered copy of every vector plus roughly 4MB of centroids. The persistent footprint on the SAN is 16.24GB, 18 times the source text, before the operational space Oracle needs around it: 15 to 23GB of TEMP while the index builds, and 4 to 8GB of UNDO and about 15GB of REDO during ingest.

The multiplier scales with the embedding model: Broadcom extrapolates from the same method, putting a 768-dimension Cohere v3 model (also measured) at 4.8x the source, a 384-dimension MiniLM at 9.6x, and a 4,096-dimension Mistral model at 32.5x. Chunk size matters as much as width, since a wide vector over a long passage amplifies less than the same vector over a short one, and quantized indexes shrink the index share.

None of this is specific to FlashSystem or to Oracle. The amplification happens inside the database before the array sees a byte, and every vector index on every platform carries a copy of the vectors, so it belongs in the capacity budget the day a vector project is approved, alongside the GPUs. What the array decides is how much of that growth it can hold: IBM’s fifth-generation FlashCore Module runs to 105.6TB per module, which puts 3.3PB raw in a 2U enclosure on the largest FlashSystem models, 11.8PB effective by IBM’s figure, so a vector tier can grow in place for years before a partition has to move.

IBM’s sizing model for the healthcare application that follows runs the other way for images: 100GB of X-rays yields roughly 2GB inside the database, since only the embeddings and case metadata live there. Text is the expensive case: 100GB of chunked clinical text lands at 860GB to 1.2TB, most of it HNSW index. The sizing input is the chunk count and the model width; the source corpus is a poor guide. Embeddings also compress less than rows, 1.2x to 2x vs. 2x to 4x for relational data, per IBM’s experience, so FlashCore Module data reduction recovers less of the growth, and every re-embed needs the TEMP space again.

IBM’s practical rule is to measure before committing. Load 1 to 5 percent of the real corpus with the production embedding model and chunking settings, measure the actual bytes per vector, then scale linearly, and repeat the exercise whenever the model, the dimension count, or the chunking policy changes.

IBM built the application for this validation as a radiology and gastroenterology assistant called RAD-AI. It is a sample application with production-style requirements, and in this paper it demonstrates a complete inference pipeline on the same array and fabric the earlier sections measured. A clinician enters a patient’s age, sex, and presenting complaint, uploads a chest X-ray or endoscopy image, and receives a structured report built from the most similar prior cases in the archive.

The archive holds 112,120 chest X-rays from the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset and more than 10,000 GI endoscopy images from HyperKvasir, including per-frame vectors from 367 full endoscopy videos, for more than 172,000 pre-embedded cases. Each image becomes a 768-dimensional vector from a CLIP ViT-L/14 model running inside Oracle AI Database 26ai through its ONNX runtime, so the embedding lands in the same transaction as the row that holds it. The raw images stay in object storage; the vectors and case metadata live in Oracle.

At query time, Oracle runs an approximate nearest-neighbor search by cosine distance across the archive and returns the closest cases, along with their original findings, diagnoses, and outcomes. That retrieved set is the context for Llama 3, served by Ollama on one of the H100 GPUs in the Supermicro server, which writes the report: a clinical priority, a findings summary, a ranked differential diagnosis, and recommended actions, with the matching cases listed beneath it. Endoscopy follows the same path and adds a clinical note; for video, the pipeline embeds frame-by-frame so it can track a lesion along the GI tract.

The application runs two workloads against the same FlashSystem volumes. The transactional workload covers logins, report storage, audit logging, and sessions; the vector workload performs high fan-out random reads across the embedding tables and case metadata, matching the generator profile in the I/O QoS demonstration. IBM’s deployment sets the volume throttles described earlier so a batch re-embedding job cannot slow a clinician entering a case, and the ransomware detection and partition migration shown above apply to these volumes unchanged.

The resource-heavy step is building the archive, which IBM measured by embedding the full 112,120-image chest X-ray set twice with the same model and the same VECTOR(768, FLOAT32) target. With the ONNX model running inside the database on the host CPUs, the pipeline sustained 3.41 images per second at 0.272 seconds per embedding, and the full set took 9.1 hours. Moving the model to Oracle’s Private AI Services container on the second server raised throughput to 8.55 images per second (0.097 seconds per image), and the same ingest finished in 3.6 hours.

Preprocessing (about 0.019 seconds per image) and the Oracle insert (under a millisecond) were identical on both runs, so the 2.5x gain comes entirely from where the model executes. The Private AI Services embedding service runs on a CPU ONNX runtime, so the H100s in that server sat out this test; the gain came from taking the model off the database host, and the GPU’s share of the pipeline is the index build covered next.

IBM measured these figures in the Colorado lab; we did not run or audit the test. The practical takeaway is that the first embedding of an archive, and every re-embed after a model change, is a batch job measured in hours, while the retrieval that follows is a CPU and storage job measured in milliseconds.

The same container also handles index construction. Oracle 26ai can send an HNSW build to the container’s Vector Index Service, which uses NVIDIA cuVS on the GPU to build the neighbor graph before returning the completed index to the database. Searches then run without GPU involvement. In IBM’s recording, the baseline HNSW build (32 neighbors, efConstruction 200) took 8.47 seconds in the database and 2.26 seconds with the offload, a 3.7x reduction. That run used a small demonstration table, so it confirms the path works on this configuration; we still need to measure the clinical-scale number.

The application demonstrates the division of labor at the heart of this paper. The GPU server hosts the language model and, during archive builds or rebuilds, the embedding and indexing services. The database stores vectors alongside the records they describe, while the array and fabric handle retrieval reads and transactions. No step in the retrieval path uses an external API, and patient data never leaves the data center.

IBM chose healthcare as the vertical to prove the concept, and nothing in the pattern is specific to it. Swap the X-ray archive for claims histories, maintenance records, or a product catalog and the same three pieces carry over: vectors stored beside the records they describe, generation on the GPU server, and retrieval and transactions on one array. Any industry running inference against data it already holds lands on the same architecture.

The validation continues on the same hardware: Phase 2 moves the inference engine’s KV cache from GPU memory onto FlashSystem over the same Fibre Channel fabric, so a long-context model keeps more of its working set in reach; the next paper in this series covers that work. IBM is also building a content-aware refresh pipeline, with IBM Storage Scale AFM and Kafka feeding new documents into in-database ONNX vectorization as they arrive, so the vector index tracks its sources without a batch re-embed. IBM also plans to extend the same storage validation to the other multi-model databases that have added vector search.

Phase 2 also puts the security layer to work on new data. When the KV cache moves onto FlashSystem, a healthcare model’s working context (patient history included) crosses the same Fibre Channel links as the vector index and the transactional records. Emulex SecureHBAs encrypt it in flight end to end, from the host adapter to the storage array, with the Brocade Gen 8 fabric carrying the encrypted traffic transparently while also offering post-quantum cryptography for inter-switch link (ISL) and long-distance traffic. Each phase adds a workload to the fabric without adding a path where data travels in the clear.
Leaderboard: IBM’s profile on our Best Storage Arrays page now covers FlashSystem block storage alongside Storage Scale.

articles.title: One Array for AI: Inside the IBM FlashSystem and Broadcom Fibre Channel Architecture Behind Oracle AI Database 26ai
articles.summary: The biggest AI infrastructure decision many enterprises make in the next year won’t be a GPU investment; it will be a database upgrade. Oracle AI Database 26ai is the long-term support release Oracle is steering its 19c installed base toward. 26ai puts vector search in the same engine that holds transactions. When the vector index The post One Array for AI: Inside the IBM FlashSystem and Broadcom Fibre Channel Architecture Behind Oracle AI Database 26ai appeared first on StorageReview.com .
bodyEvidence: The biggest AI infrastructure decision many enterprises make in the next year won’t be a GPU investment; it will be a database upgrade. Oracle AI Database 26ai is the long-term support release Oracle is steering its 19c installed base toward. 26ai puts vector search in the same engine that holds transactions. When the vector index lives in the database, the block array and the SAN fabric behind it become AI infrastructure, carrying retrieval traffic alongside the transactions they already serve.

Oracle built 26ai around that idea: a native VECTOR data type, SQL vector search functions, in-database model execution through ONNX, and SELECT AI for natural language queries, all in an LTS release the company enumerates at more than 300 new features. In practice, a DBA can generate embeddings, store them next to the rows they describe, and run a similarity search within the same transaction scope as an order lookup. There’s no separate vector store to run, no synchronization pipeline to maintain, and no second copy of regulated data living outside the audit trail.

IBM cites IDC on the trend: “Integrated vector databases are the clear platform of choice for storing and querying vector embeddings, as organizations favor unified, governed environments for agentic AI.” IBM and Broadcom’s customers want to extend the database they already trust before standing up a new one alongside it. Oracle is not alone in this direction. DB-Engines’ October 2026 popularity ranking lists the top four relational and multi-model engines: Oracle, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, and PostgreSQL, and all four have added vector types or vector search, natively or through extensions such as pgvector. IBM chose to start its validation work with Oracle primarily because of its market leadership, though the storage argument in this piece applies to the others as well.

The arguments for keeping block storage on-prem haven’t changed with AI in the picture: the data that makes an AI deployment useful, such as patient records, claims, orders, and trades, can’t leave. Copying it to a dedicated AI platform means paying for storage twice, accepting that the copy drifts from the production cluster, and losing the governance controls that made the original legally defensible. Keeping retrieval inside the database avoids all three. The array that serves a sub-millisecond row lookup now also serves a vector similarity scan for a clinician and a backup stream at the same time.

IBM Storage and Broadcom’s Fibre Channel (FC) group set out to validate that mixed-workload case, and built an environment around Oracle AI Database 26ai on IBM FlashSystem with Broadcom’s Brocade Gen 8 SAN fabric and Emulex 64G SecureHBAs . They then worked through the questions an infrastructure team had been asking: what is the impact on transactional latency when a vector workload starts next to it, the effect of fabric speed on vector search throughput, the capacity consumed by embeddings, the effectiveness of ransomware detection when targeting an RMAN backup volume, and what are the requirements for adding a host to the SAN without a zoning ticket?

None of this says AI workloads in general belong on block storage. Enterprises will keep file and object arrays for the unstructured estate: documents, images, video, training sets, and model checkpoints that never lived in a database and likely never will. In the healthcare demonstration that follows, IBM keeps the raw X-ray images in object storage while storing only the embeddings and case metadata in Oracle. What changes is the burden on the array, which now carries several workloads with very different I/O profiles at the same time.

The relational tier is the most familiar one: millions of random 4KB to 16KB I/Os per second, row lookups and commits that need to land in microseconds, heavy write concurrency from redo, undo, and checkpoint traffic, and a tail latency that stays predictable because a user-facing application is waiting on it. RMAN, Oracle’s backup utility, is the opposite: a sequential stream that needs headroom to finish inside its window without disturbing the first workload. Both are well understood, and IBM’s arrays are tuned for them.

The vector tier is harder to characterize because large tables of vector embeddings can make vector search look like a bandwidth-intensive workload: a large sequential scan. IBM’s characterization of the Oracle 26ai vector path is closer to OLTP. Each hop through the index is a roughly 4KB random read; the query path is IOPS-bound and latency-sensitive, and reads dominate because writes live in a separate ingest and index-build phase.

Bandwidth matters in bursts, when an index is built or a corpus is re-embedded, and those bursts tend to be quite large. That split is the core of the mixed-I/O problem: on the query path, the vector workload competes with transactions for the same queues, making isolation a quality-of-service concern. And the bursty phases are where fabric bandwidth becomes the ceiling, as the 32G versus 64G results later in this piece show.

IBM and Broadcom built one environment for this validation in Broadcom’s Colorado AI lab. The storage is an IBM FlashSystem 9000 series array running IBM Storage Virtualize 9.1.3 with 24 FlashCore Modules, presenting 64G Fibre Channel ports to a pair of Brocade Gen 8 G820 SAN switches. The database host is a dual-socket Intel Xeon 6767P server with two 2-port Emulex LPe38102 64G SecureHBAs, running Oracle AI Database 26ai on ASM with no GPU in the storage path; IBM Storage Insights watches the array.

We ran the fabric and capacity results, the 32G versus 64G vector search comparison, and the footprint measurements using VectorDBBench against the BioASQ 1M dataset on that host alone. The same configuration also supports the application workload. A Supermicro 821GE-TNHR with two Xeon Platinum 8470 processors and eight NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs hosts the healthcare application and its language model. The software stack includes Oracle’s in-database ONNX embedding, Ollama serving Llama 3, and NVIDIA cuVS. A Broadcom Tomahawk 5 switch and Thor 2 400GbE NICs connect the two servers. The I/O QoS, multi-tenancy, ransomware detection, and healthcare demonstrations ran in this environment.

According to IBM, the FlashSystem family (the 5300 and 5600, 7300 and 7600, and 9500 and 9600) runs the same Storage Virtualize software, and the functions demonstrated here, including I/O throttling, AutoZoning, ransomware detection, Policy-Based HA, and storage partition migration, work the same way with Oracle AI Database 26ai on any of those arrays at the same code level. Performance and density vary by model and FlashCore Module generation, so every figure in this piece belongs to the system it was measured on.

The first question IBM and Broadcom set out to answer is the one every DBA asks when a vector workload is proposed for the production array: what happens to the core transactions? IBM ran it as two demonstrations on the FlashSystem 9000 series array using volume-level I/O throttles, the mechanism behind what IBM calls I/O QoS. The database was laid out across 30 volumes: 15 for the OLTP tablespaces (ORCL16 through ORCL30) under Swingbench Order Entry at 192 users, and 15 for the vector tables (ORCL31 through ORCL45) under a 200-thread synthetic generator running top-k 500 similarity queries, with Storage Insights charting each volume group.

With OLTP running alone, each OLTP volume held a flat 20,500 ops/s. When the vector generator started, the vector volumes climbed to about 73,000 ops/s each within a minute, and the OLTP volumes fell to about 13,000, a 37 percent drop with nothing changed on the transactional side. The vector search path is 4KB random reads at the same block size as the transactions, so it hits the same queues and takes whatever the array will give it.

A 45,000 IOPS cap on each vector volume, one line of mkthrottle at the CLI, pulled the vector volumes to the limit and lifted OLTP back to about 17,000 ops/s. Removing the cap reversed it, and when the vector run ended, OLTP returned to 20,500. The dashboard tracked the same thing in aggregate: 1.28 million IOPS unthrottled and roughly 950,000 under the cap, which, within a few percent, is the per-volume rate times 30 volumes.

The second demo is the configuration IBM expects would deploy in production: caps set first, 45,000 IOPS per vector volume and 20,000 per OLTP volume, then both workloads launched together. The vector volumes ran at their ceiling, the OLTP volumes settled at about 12,200 ops/s and stayed flat for the length of the run, and the array held 870,000 IOPS (800,000 read, 70,000 write) at 377 microseconds and 6.9GB/s on 25% CPU. The OLTP cap sat above the workload’s demand and never engaged; it’s there so a runaway on either side can’t starve the other.

Swingbench held its 192 users at about 1.19 million transactions per minute, roughly 19,500 TPS, for the length of the run. The generator was tuned to saturate its volumes, so its per-query latency isn’t an application benchmark. Over the 30-minute run, it completed 35,672 queries at 19.8 per second, with a median latency of about 10 seconds and a p99 of 14.3 seconds against a 15-second application timeout; 99 queries (0.28 percent) hit that timeout, and the transactions never noticed any of it.

A FlashSystem throttle is a volume ceiling enforced at the array regardless of host or path, with an optional bandwidth limit alongside the IOPS limit; it caps the neighbor and reserves nothing. The cap is a sizing exercise: 15 vector volumes at 45,000 IOPS is 675,000 IOPS of vector headroom, which left this array’s OLTP volumes what they needed. A different array or mix moves the number around some. Set the vector cap where the transactions hold their latency, and the vector workload gets everything above it.

Sophos’s 2024 survey of 2,974 organizations hit by ransomware found that 94 percent saw the attackers go after their backups, that the attempt succeeded 57 percent of the time, and that median recovery costs ran eight times higher when it did. IBM built the test on the same premise, backups first and production second, and aimed the attack at the RMAN backup target while leaving the database volumes alone. RMAN wrote its backup sets to FlashSystem volumes, a ransomware simulator was run against them, and the array was left to notice on its own, with no host agent in the path.

Detection happens inside the drives: FCM4 and FCM5 FlashCore Modules compute entropy and compressibility on every write as it lands, along with block size, address, and rewrite patterns, and every two seconds pass a per-volume summary to an inference engine inside Storage Virtualize (8.6.3 or later with FCM firmware 4.1 or later). The model raises alerts in the FlashSystem GUI and IBM Storage Insights Pro, forwards them to Storage Defender or a SIEM, and is patchable on its own, so a retrained model ships as a small security update with no firmware upgrade.

Because the analysis runs on the module, it keeps working even when the host is what’s compromised. Encrypted output is high-entropy and stops compressing, and that shows up in the statistics whether the attacker changes file extensions, encrypts only every other block, or slows the rate to hide from an endpoint agent.

During validation, RMAN wrote the backup over 16 parallel channels, with each backup set capped at 150GB, and the database sat on 15 x 200GB disks per ASM disk group for OLTP and vector data. IBM ran the attack against that backup target, and the alert reached Storage Insights in under 60 seconds, which is within the detection window IBM publishes for the feature. Storage Insights flagged all 31 volumes in the volume group, since an alert on one volume marks the whole group as a threat. The response is Safeguarded Copy, and the array handled it without an operator: the FlashSystem took an immutable snapshot of the affected volume group the moment the threat was raised and extended the retention of the last-known good snapshot at the same time. The lsanomalydetection output from the array shows the configuration behind that: inference engine 8.0 with model 0.3.42.0, anomaly_snapshot on, 30 days of retention on the new snapshot, and 30 days added to the last good one. Storage Virtualize also marks the suspect snapshot so nobody restores from it, leaving a clean restore point from before the encryption began.

The fabric also carries a security layer. Broadcom builds post-quantum cryptography into Brocade Gen 8 platforms, the Emulex SecureHBAs encrypt data in flight from host to storage array across that fabric, and FCIA’s new FC-SP-3 standard sets the quantum-ready security baseline for Fibre Channel as a whole.

From there, FlashSystem builds peer zones, allowing host initiators to reach the target port but not each other, under a predictable IBM_SV_ name that marks them as array-managed.

Setup starts in the Fibre Channel port view, which now shows the switch each port connects to, whether the port is AutoZone capable, and whether its connectivity is symmetric, meaning the same port ID on every node lands on the same fabric. A topology view maps that in color, and only green ports that are active, AutoZone capable, and symmetric support AutoZoning. Asymmetric ports stay out even if otherwise capable, since the GUI warns it can compromise redundancy and failover.

Host creation starts from an Unconfigured hosts list, filled through FDMI, which reports each HBA’s host name, operating system, and ports to the fabric. In IBM’s walkthrough, the Add Host dialog opened with the server name, operating system, and both HBA ports of a host that had no zones yet already populated; the admin picked an AutoZone-enabled port set, which defines the target ports the host can reach, and clicked Add. FlashSystem paired its target ports with the host initiators, pushed the zones to both switches, and the host came online with four paths across two fabrics.
