The same automation applies when hosts need paths to a second array for storage partition migration or Policy-Based HA (PBHA). The SAN team still controls which target ports participate, since nothing happens on a port until they enable TDZ. Consequently, adding a host no longer waits on a zoning change.

Policy-Based HA (PBHA) synchronously replicates a storage partition between two FlashSystem arrays at metro distance, with active-active host access at both sites. IBM says the feature is designed for zero RPO and for a storage failover that a properly clustered Oracle deployment can ride through without data loss. When the failed site comes back, the data resyncs and the workload moves back without an outage.

The FlashSystem Grid feature federates up to 32 FlashSystem arrays under one management view, and storage partition migration moves a partition, with its volumes, volume groups, and hosts, from one array to another without application downtime. For Oracle, IBM points to hardware refresh, draining a system before a firmware update, and moving a vector partition to a system with more capacity as the embedding set grows. A system migrates one partition at a time over Fibre Channel or high-speed Ethernet; hosts can connect over Fibre Channel, iSCSI, or NVMe/TCP, and a partition already configured for PBHA is not eligible for migration.

The Storage Insights placement advisor handles planning for the same grid. Given a workload’s capacity, growth rate, I/O profile, and latency target, it scores every system in the grid, ranks the best fit before anything is provisioned, and can also recommend a migration when it spots a CPU or IOPS imbalance. Migration and placement both use Storage Insights Pro, with every grid system registered to the same Storage Insights tenant.

Multi-tenancy lets a DBA team and an AI team share that grid without sharing administration. In IBM’s walkthrough, an administrator created two tenants on the same array (Tenant_Scale and Tenant_oracle_ai) and gave each one a system, a user group with a tenant role, and a first user. They then built a storage partition for each with a separate volume group, volumes, and host mappings. The GUI offers to configure replication as soon as a new partition exists. Logged in as the Tenant_Scale user, the GUI showed only that tenant’s partition and resources, with nothing belonging to Tenant_oracle_ai, and the same check from the Tenant_oracle_ai side returned the same result.

The one variable IBM and Broadcom changed in this testing, on purpose, was the fabric. The same array, host, and Emulex LPe38102 SecureHBAs ran VectorDBBench against the BioASQ 1M dataset (one million 1,024-dimension vectors from the biomedical question-answering corpus) twice: once with the two HBA ports at 32G and once at 64G, through the same Brocade G820 switches. Everything else, from the 16 ASM volumes to the 4GB SGA, stayed put, so the difference between the two runs is the Fibre Channel generation and nothing else.

The search phase of this benchmark is a read-only scan: Oracle’s IVF_FLAT index routes each query to a cluster of partitions and reads them in full, and with 1,024-dimension FLOAT32 vectors, that is a bandwidth workload. On two 32G ports, host-side reads leveled at 6.3GB/s, the line rate of the pair, and the search curve flattened at 43.7 queries per second with 20 threads. On two 64G ports, the same host read at 12.5GB/s and kept scaling to 85.0 QPS at 80 threads, 95% more throughput from the same storage.

Latency tells the other part of the 64G story: at one thread the two fabrics are within 8% of each other, 0.107 seconds against 0.099, because a single query never fills either pipe. From five threads on, however, the 32G run queues: average latency doubles the 64G figure at every step, and at 80 threads p99 reaches 4.08 seconds against 1.14. A saturated FC fabric doesn’t fail; it queues every query, and that wait shows up as tail latency.

The load phase moved too; ingesting the million vectors took 94.1 seconds on 32G and 84.5 on 64G, and the IVF_FLAT index build took 139.6 seconds against 108.4, 28.8% longer on the slower fabric, for a total load of 233.7 seconds against 193.0. Recall and NDCG were within 0.1% across the two runs (83.81% and 84.42% on 32G, 83.95% and 84.56% on 64G), so the fabric changed how quickly answers arrived. For a database that has been on 32G since deployment, the HBA and switch upgrade is an obvious opportunity to deliver more performance.

Vector search changes the capacity math before it changes performance. An embedding is a fixed-width numeric copy of a chunk of source data, and for text that copy is usually larger than the chunk it describes: a 1,000-byte passage becomes a 1,024-dimension FLOAT32 vector of 4,096 bytes before the database adds a row to hold it. The team calls this vector storage amplification, and measured it on the same BioASQ 1M dataset used in the fabric comparison.

The source text behind the million vectors is 0.90GB. In Oracle 26ai, it became a 7.67GB vector table, including about 0.3GB of row overhead, and the IVF_FLAT index added 8.57GB on top because it keeps a second, clustered copy of every vector plus roughly 4MB of centroids. The persistent footprint on the SAN is 16.24GB, 18 times the source text, before the operational space Oracle needs around it: 15 to 23GB of TEMP while the index builds, and 4 to 8GB of UNDO and about 15GB of REDO during ingest.

The multiplier scales with the embedding model: Broadcom extrapolates from the same method, putting a 768-dimension Cohere v3 model (also measured) at 4.8x the source, a 384-dimension MiniLM at 9.6x, and a 4,096-dimension Mistral model at 32.5x. Chunk size matters as much as width, since a wide vector over a long passage amplifies less than the same vector over a short one, and quantized indexes shrink the index share.

None of this is specific to FlashSystem or to Oracle. The amplification happens inside the database before the array sees a byte, and every vector index on every platform carries a copy of the vectors, so it belongs in the capacity budget the day a vector project is approved, alongside the GPUs. What the array decides is how much of that growth it can hold: IBM’s fifth-generation FlashCore Module runs to 105.6TB per module, which puts 3.3PB raw in a 2U enclosure on the largest FlashSystem models, 11.8PB effective by IBM’s figure, so a vector tier can grow in place for years before a partition has to move.

IBM’s sizing model for the healthcare application that follows runs the other way for images: 100GB of X-rays yields roughly 2GB inside the database, since only the embeddings and case metadata live there. Text is the expensive case: 100GB of chunked clinical text lands at 860GB to 1.2TB, most of it HNSW index. The sizing input is the chunk count and the model width; the source corpus is a poor guide. Embeddings also compress less than rows, 1.2x to 2x vs. 2x to 4x for relational data, per IBM’s experience, so FlashCore Module data reduction recovers less of the growth, and every re-embed needs the TEMP space again.

IBM’s practical rule is to measure before committing. Load 1 to 5 percent of the real corpus with the production embedding model and chunking settings, measure the actual bytes per vector, then scale linearly, and repeat the exercise whenever the model, the dimension count, or the chunking policy changes.

IBM built the application for this validation as a radiology and gastroenterology assistant called RAD-AI. It is a sample application with production-style requirements, and in this paper it demonstrates a complete inference pipeline on the same array and fabric the earlier sections measured. A clinician enters a patient’s age, sex, and presenting complaint, uploads a chest X-ray or endoscopy image, and receives a structured report built from the most similar prior cases in the archive.

The archive holds 112,120 chest X-rays from the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset and more than 10,000 GI endoscopy images from HyperKvasir, including per-frame vectors from 367 full endoscopy videos, for more than 172,000 pre-embedded cases. Each image becomes a 768-dimensional vector from a CLIP ViT-L/14 model running inside Oracle AI Database 26ai through its ONNX runtime, so the embedding lands in the same transaction as the row that holds it. The raw images stay in object storage; the vectors and case metadata live in Oracle.

At query time, Oracle runs an approximate nearest-neighbor search by cosine distance across the archive and returns the closest cases, along with their original findings, diagnoses, and outcomes. That retrieved set is the context for Llama 3, served by Ollama on one of the H100 GPUs in the Supermicro server, which writes the report: a clinical priority, a findings summary, a ranked differential diagnosis, and recommended actions, with the matching cases listed beneath it. Endoscopy follows the same path and adds a clinical note; for video, the pipeline embeds frame-by-frame so it can track a lesion along the GI tract.

The application runs two workloads against the same FlashSystem volumes. The transactional workload covers logins, report storage, audit logging, and sessions; the vector workload performs high fan-out random reads across the embedding tables and case metadata, matching the generator profile in the I/O QoS demonstration. IBM’s deployment sets the volume throttles described earlier so a batch re-embedding job cannot slow a clinician entering a case, and the ransomware detection and partition migration shown above apply to these volumes unchanged.

The resource-heavy step is building the archive, which IBM measured by embedding the full 112,120-image chest X-ray set twice with the same model and the same VECTOR(768, FLOAT32) target. With the ONNX model running inside the database on the host CPUs, the pipeline sustained 3.41 images per second at 0.272 seconds per embedding, and the full set took 9.1 hours. Moving the model to Oracle’s Private AI Services container on the second server raised throughput to 8.55 images per second (0.097 seconds per image), and the same ingest finished in 3.6 hours.

Preprocessing (about 0.019 seconds per image) and the Oracle insert (under a millisecond) were identical on both runs, so the 2.5x gain comes entirely from where the model executes. The Private AI Services embedding service runs on a CPU ONNX runtime, so the H100s in that server sat out this test; the gain came from taking the model off the database host, and the GPU’s share of the pipeline is the index build covered next.

IBM measured these figures in the Colorado lab; we did not run or audit the test. The practical takeaway is that the first embedding of an archive, and every re-embed after a model change, is a batch job measured in hours, while the retrieval that follows is a CPU and storage job measured in milliseconds.

The same container also handles index construction. Oracle 26ai can send an HNSW build to the container’s Vector Index Service, which uses NVIDIA cuVS on the GPU to build the neighbor graph before returning the completed index to the database. Searches then run without GPU involvement. In IBM’s recording, the baseline HNSW build (32 neighbors, efConstruction 200) took 8.47 seconds in the database and 2.26 seconds with the offload, a 3.7x reduction. That run used a small demonstration table, so it confirms the path works on this configuration; we still need to measure the clinical-scale number.

The application demonstrates the division of labor at the heart of this paper. The GPU server hosts the language model and, during archive builds or rebuilds, the embedding and indexing services. The database stores vectors alongside the records they describe, while the array and fabric handle retrieval reads and transactions. No step in the retrieval path uses an external API, and patient data never leaves the data center.

IBM chose healthcare as the vertical to prove the concept, and nothing in the pattern is specific to it. Swap the X-ray archive for claims histories, maintenance records, or a product catalog and the same three pieces carry over: vectors stored beside the records they describe, generation on the GPU server, and retrieval and transactions on one array. Any industry running inference against data it already holds lands on the same architecture.

The validation continues on the same hardware: Phase 2 moves the inference engine’s KV cache from GPU memory onto FlashSystem over the same Fibre Channel fabric, so a long-context model keeps more of its working set in reach; the next paper in this series covers that work. IBM is also building a content-aware refresh pipeline, with IBM Storage Scale AFM and Kafka feeding new documents into in-database ONNX vectorization as they arrive, so the vector index tracks its sources without a batch re-embed. IBM also plans to extend the same storage validation to the other multi-model databases that have added vector search.

Phase 2 also puts the security layer to work on new data. When the KV cache moves onto FlashSystem, a healthcare model’s working context (patient history included) crosses the same Fibre Channel links as the vector index and the transactional records. Emulex SecureHBAs encrypt it in flight end to end, from the host adapter to the storage array, with the Brocade Gen 8 fabric carrying the encrypted traffic transparently while also offering post-quantum cryptography for inter-switch link (ISL) and long-distance traffic. Each phase adds a workload to the fabric without adding a path where data travels in the clear.

rssBodyEvidence: AMD says the first AMD Helios rackscale systems are installed and under test at Meta, with a broader deployment to follow, and that the two companies have aligned product roadmaps around Meta’s workloads across EPYC CPUs, Instinct GPUs, Pensando networking, and ROCm. The same announcement puts EPYC behind Meta’s Muse personal AI agent, adds Day-0 AMD support for the Muse Spark Open and Muse Glimmer models, and commits AMD to a $1 billion investment in Meta’s equity offering.

“AMD has been a key partner in building out the compute that’s running our frontier models,” said Mark Zuckerberg, founder and CEO, Meta. “We’re making big investments in the computing power that will enable us to bring personal superintelligence to everyone, and AMD plays an important role in that.” Lisa Su, Chair and CEO, AMD, said: “With Helios now running at Meta, we are taking that partnership to a new scale in the superintelligence era.”

AMD gives no rack count or site for the Helios installation and no date for the broader deployment beyond “the near future.” On the CPU side, Meta has deployed millions of EPYC processors across multiple generations and is a lead customer for 6th Gen EPYC , which supports the dedicated computing environments behind Muse. The companies are also collaborating on future EPYC generations, including the part AMD calls “Verano.”

Meta runs AMD Instinct GPUs in production for training, ranking, and recommendation engines. The custom silicon is what separates this from a volume purchase: Meta was an early definition customer for the Instinct MI450 architecture and will deploy a custom Instinct GPU optimized for its workloads. AMD says the collaboration is informing future platforms, including the Instinct MI500 series and next-generation rack-scale systems.

The software work runs through PyTorch so that ROCm support is in place when a developer pulls the framework. AMD and Meta have optimized recommendation model training on Instinct MI350X GPUs and are contributing the improvements back to PyTorch, Triton, and ROCm. On the model side, AMD delivered Day-0 support for Muse Spark Open on Instinct GPUs, and for Muse Glimmer on Ryzen AI PCs and Radeon GPUs, which puts that model on client hardware from the start.

rssBodyEvidence: NVIDIA and Oracle plan to expand Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Superclusters with NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems to multi-gigawatt scale, and both Vera Rubin NVL72 and NVIDIA Vera CPUs are now generally available on OCI. The companies announced the pair at Oracle AI World. The expansion is a plan; the general availability is the part customers can buy now, aimed at the GPU-heavy work of training and serving frontier models and the CPU-heavy work agents do between model calls, with CPU and GPU capacity scaled independently.

The proof point the companies offer is OpenAI, which has trained and served GPT-6 Astra in Abilene on an OCI Supercluster with more than 100,000 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. “As our frontier models advance, we need infrastructure that can keep pace,” said Sreekanth Pothanis, engineering leader, compute infra at OpenAI. “NVIDIA Vera Rubin on OCI gives us the computing performance and scale to accelerate model training and serve increasingly demanding AI workloads.”

Each Vera Rubin NVL72 rack connects 72 GPUs through NVLink scale-up networking. OCI Superclusters combine those racks with Oracle Acceleron networking, NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet with Spectrum-6 switches and BlueField-4 DPUs, and gigawatt-class power and cooling. Oracle says the multiplanar network scales across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. The Vera Rubin build-out extends the GB200 and GB300 NVL72 systems already on OCI, and the companies point to the common CUDA foundation as the reason models and workloads carry across generations.

OCI also plans to add NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 , an x86 server with eight Rubin GPUs connected through NVLink. The planned configuration carries two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 CPUs, 4TB of DDR5 memory, and 6.4 Tbps of RDMA networking, and Oracle positions it for training, fine-tuning, and inference where a customer wants Rubin GPUs in a smaller footprint without giving up x86 application compatibility. Neither company gave a date for it.

The Vera CPU offering targets the work an agent does between model calls: tool calls, code execution, and data retrieval. Those steps run on CPUs, and when they run slowly the GPUs sit waiting. NVIDIA and Oracle say Vera’s single-thread performance speeds up individual tool calls and code execution while its memory bandwidth keeps cores fed as agents run concurrent tasks, which together cut GPU idle time. Neither company gives performance figures or test conditions for the claim.

OCI Kubernetes Engine lets customers scale CPU and GPU pools independently, and Oracle Acceleron provides hardware-based isolation for workloads running untrusted, AI-generated code. OpenAI is among the early-access customers. “NVIDIA Vera CPUs on OCI deliver the world-class loaded performance needed to execute code and run tools across our rapidly growing agentic sandbox workloads,” said Uday Ruddarraju, chief technology officer of compute at OpenAI. “We are bringing Vera into production on OCI to support these workloads at scale.” The scale of that deployment was not given.

“AI factories must be productive, durable and fungible,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, describing the goal as infrastructure that stays useful through software advances and serves different models and workloads as demand changes. Mahesh Thiagarajan, president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, framed the pairing of Vera Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs with Acceleron networking as a way to keep GPUs productive and secure as customer needs grow.

rssBodyEvidence: IBM FlashSystem 5600, 7600, and 9600 arrays built on the fifth-generation IBM FlashCore Module now detect data exfiltration inside the drive, next to the ransomware encryption detection the modules already run. IBM says the module learns each volume’s normal read pattern, flags reads that break from it, and confirms a suspected event over a 30-minute confidence window with a validated false-positive rate below 1%. The capability is available starting in October 2026 on eligible configurations running firmware 9.1.2 or later.

The case IBM makes is that recovery answers the wrong question when data has already left. Recovery brings the volumes back, but it cannot tell an operator what was read out before the encryption started or how large the exposure is. IBM cites Google Cloud’s M-Trends 2026 for attackers typically spending 11 to 14 days inside a network before deploying ransomware, and its Cost of a Data Breach 2026 report for an average of 247 days to identify a breach.

Exfiltration is harder to catch than encryption because it is meant to look like ordinary reads. The FlashCore Module analyzes every I/O at the drive, builds a baseline for each volume, and recognizes routine backup passes and analytics scans so a scheduled full read does not trip an alert. Because the analysis runs in the module, it does not depend on endpoint agents or host logs an attacker may control, requires no application changes, and IBM says it adds no measurable performance impact.

“The future of cyber resilience is not simply recovering after an attack,” said Sam Werner, General Manager, IBM Storage. He framed the goal as identifying risk before damage occurs, with earlier insight into potential data theft and a faster response. Laurence Horrocks-Barlow, Technical Director at OCF Limited, described storage-layer detection as another stage of defense: “The sooner you know something is wrong, the sooner you can act.”

The second change targets harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks, where encrypted data stolen today is held until quantum hardware can break the key. FlashSystem keeps AES-256 for data at rest, and the fifth-generation FlashCore Module adds ML-KEM under FIPS 203 and ML-DSA under FIPS 204, two algorithms developed with IBM researchers. ML-KEM runs in hybrid mode to transport the unlock PIN to the module, and hybrid ML-DSA signatures verify firmware authenticity.

IBM says Secure HBAs will carry the post-quantum protections into the Fibre Channel data path and enable quantum-safe, session-level encryption on the fabric, without affecting efficiency, performance, or the ransomware detection running in the modules. IBM has not given a date for the HBA piece, and the session-level encryption is described as a future capability.

FlashSystem.ai, introduced with the 5600, 7600, and 9600 launch, picks up advisory capabilities in this update: contextual recommendations, task context that carries across management sessions, and suggested next-best actions. Administrators work in natural language, can see the reasoning behind a recommendation, and keep approval authority through policy-based governance. IBM puts the effort reduction for routine provisioning at up to 90%, a figure from lab-controlled evaluations of multi-volume provisioning with Safeguarded Copy and disaster recovery policies.

Laurence Horrocks-Barlow, Technical Director at OCF Limited, described storage-layer detection as another stage of defense: “The sooner you know something is wrong, the sooner you can act.”

The second change targets harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks, where encrypted data stolen today is held until quantum hardware can break the key. FlashSystem keeps AES-256 for data at rest, and the fifth-generation FlashCore Module adds ML-KEM under FIPS 203 and ML-DSA under FIPS 204, two algorithms developed with IBM researchers. ML-KEM runs in hybrid mode to transport the unlock PIN to the module, and hybrid ML-DSA signatures verify firmware authenticity.

IBM says Secure HBAs will carry the post-quantum protections into the Fibre Channel data path and enable quantum-safe, session-level encryption on the fabric, without affecting efficiency, performance, or the ransomware detection running in the modules. IBM has not given a date for the HBA piece, and the session-level encryption is described as a future capability.

FlashSystem.ai, introduced with the 5600, 7600, and 9600 launch, picks up advisory capabilities in this update: contextual recommendations, task context that carries across management sessions, and suggested next-best actions. Administrators work in natural language, can see the reasoning behind a recommendation, and keep approval authority through policy-based governance. IBM puts the effort reduction for routine provisioning at up to 90%, a figure from lab-controlled evaluations of multi-volume provisioning with Safeguarded Copy and disaster recovery policies.

rssBodyEvidence: Seagate announced that its Mozaic hard drives built on heat-assisted magnetic recording (HAMR) and configured for shingled magnetic recording (SMR) have been added to Broadcom’s approved vendor list for its host bus adapters, which Seagate calls the first and only SMR drives on the list. Microsoft Azure Storage has qualified the Broadcom HBA with Seagate HAMR plus SMR drives for its fleet, which gives the pairing a hyperscale proof point. The practical effect is that a buyer can order the highest-capacity Seagate drives and a Broadcom controller as a supported combination without doing the interoperability work themselves.

Seagate’s announcement names no part numbers, but Broadcom’s compatibility report for the eHBA 96xx family does. The new SMR section lists two Seagate SATA 6Gb/s models, the 32TB ST32000NM001F on firmware SR05 and the 36TB ST36000NM001M on firmware SR01, both qualified at Broadcom firmware phase MR8.17 with 512-byte logical sectors, against the eHBA 9620-16i, 9600-24i, and 9600-16i Tri-Mode adapters. Those are the SMR versions of the Exos M line on the Mozaic 3+ platform, the 3TB-per-platter HAMR design that Seagate took to 36TB with SMR.

The same report, updated the same day, also carries an SMR page for Western Digital, listing 17 Ultrastar DC HC690 models at Broadcom firmware phase MR8.18. Seagate’s drives sit one firmware phase earlier, which supports the “first” in Seagate’s claim, but Broadcom’s list no longer supports “only,” and buyers comparing the two SMR camps can now do it on the same adapter. Both lists are SATA only; no SAS SMR models appear for either vendor.

SMR overlaps adjacent tracks to raise capacity, which turns the drive into a zoned device: data is written sequentially inside zones, and the host or the drive has to manage the rewrites. Host-managed SMR drives in particular do not behave like conventional disks at the SCSI and ATA command level, and an HBA or RAID stack that does not pass the zone commands through cleanly will refuse the drive or corrupt it.

That is why SMR has lived almost entirely inside hyperscalers that write the host software themselves. When we tested the host-managed Exos X26z , Windows did not see the drive at all, a Supermicro server’s SAS bays did not detect it under Ubuntu, and it only appeared on a direct SATA cable with a zoned btrfs file system on top.

An AVL entry means Broadcom has run the drive through its interoperability suite on the named adapters and firmware, and will support the combination. Broadcom describes the HBA’s role as the communication path that lets large numbers of drives be connected, addressed, and managed by the host, and frames the SMR qualification as a path for more customers to integrate and manage high-capacity drive fleets. For an enterprise or a second-tier cloud that wants Azure-class density on a standard server, that support ticket is the difference between an SMR tier being a project and being a purchase.

Microsoft’s Azure Memory and Storage Center of Excellence completed the qualification of the Broadcom HBA with Seagate’s HAMR plus SMR drives. “At hyperscale, storage infrastructure has to meet demanding requirements for interoperability, manageability and infrastructure efficiency at scale,” said Pablo Ziperovich, general manager, Azure Memory and Storage Center of Excellence at Microsoft. “Microsoft Azure’s joint validation and qualification of Seagate and Broadcom’s SMR configuration demonstrates how these technologies can work together across large data center deployments, enabling greater storage density at a similar cost and power envelope.”

The cost and power clause is the business case, because the 36TB SMR drive fits the same 3.5-inch bay as the 30TB and 32TB CMR Exos M, so a rack of them adds capacity without adding slots or controllers, and Microsoft’s statement puts the cost and power envelope as similar. Seagate has not published pricing for the SMR models.

“High-capacity storage innovation delivers the greatest value when customers put that capacity to work efficiently,” said Jason Feist, Senior Vice President, Cloud Business at Seagate. “By pairing Seagate HAMR + SMR storage technology with Broadcom’s connectivity infrastructure, we’re helping make high-capacity SMR storage more accessible and easier to deploy as AI and cloud data demands grow.”

rssBodyEvidence: Ollama 0.40.11 gives Windows users a desktop chat application and a local model runtime for other software. Ollama has also moved beyond its original command-line interface, adding a searchable model selector, image attachments, and links to coding tools. Some controls we needed for testing still live in PowerShell and model configuration files.

We installed Ollama on our HP Z4 Rack G5 running Windows 11 Pro for Workstations, with 128GB of RAM and an NVIDIA RTX 5000 Ada Generation GPU. Using our existing Jan V3.5 4B and Jan V2 VL High GGUFs, we tested generation speed, chat, images, online search, and the local API. Ollama ran our local models well, though importing the GGUFs and collecting performance data took us out of the desktop chat. It is the third application in our local LLM series, after Jan and Open WebUI , and the results feed our Best Local LLM Tools page.

Installing Ollama on our Windows workstation was a welcome change from some of the setup headaches we encountered with other applications in this series. We downloaded the standard Windows installer, launched the application, and didn’t have to install a separate inference runtime or track down CUDA packages. A quick PowerShell check confirmed that Ollama 0.40.11 was running and that its local service was already responding at http://127.0.0.1:11434.
Ollama’s welcome screen introduces its local AI features and connections to coding tools before opening the main interface.

After we got past the welcome screen, Ollama opened to a familiar chat interface with recent conversations, Apps, and Settings in the left sidebar. The message field keeps the attachment button, Web Search, and model selector together. We could start chatting with our imported local models without creating an account, although Ollama asked us to sign in when we later tried enabling Web Search during testing.

Ollama keeps model selection fairly simple, with a dropdown that shows both installed models and others available to download. We could see our imported Jan models and Qwen3-VL alongside several cloud-based options, which were identified by a small cloud icon. There’s also a search field for finding other models, although we would have liked to see more information here, such as model sizes, quantization, and hardware requirements. Jan provides those details through its model hub, while Ollama keeps most of that information out of the main chat interface.
The model selector brings downloadable and cloud models together with the installed local models.

Getting our two benchmark models into Ollama took more work because we wanted to use the exact same GGUF files from our previous reviews, keeping the performance tests as comparable as possible. While Ollama lets you download models directly through its desktop interface, we couldn’t find an option to import GGUF files already stored on the workstation. We had to use PowerShell instead, creating a Modelfile for each model that pointed to its existing GGUF and included the sampling parameters used in our earlier tests. We then used the ollama create command to add them to Ollama’s model library.

Both imports worked without any issues, with Jan V3.5 appearing as jan-v35-sr and Jan V2 VL High as jan-v2-sr . We also downloaded Qwen3-VL 4B directly through Ollama for a separate image-analysis test.

After importing the models, we checked how Ollama identified them and whether their settings had carried over properly. Jan V2 VL High was recognized as an 8.2-billion-parameter Qwen3-VL model using Q4_K_M quantization, which matched our original file. Jan V3.5 was the exception, as the GGUF we imported was named Jan-v3.5-4B-Q4_K_XL.gguf , but Ollama reported its quantization as Q4_K_M. We left the original file unchanged; the likely reason is that Q4_K_XL is Unsloth’s dynamic quantization, built mostly from Q4_K_M layers, and the file’s metadata records that base type.

Ollama’s Settings page includes cloud access, automatic updates, network access, a model-storage path, and a context-length slider, which showed 32K when we first inspected it. Our performance tests explicitly requested 8,192 tokens through the API, so the benchmark results below used that context, not the desktop default.
The Settings page offers cloud, update, network, model-storage, and context-length options. The initial context setting shown here was 32K.

Because Ollama doesn’t offer the same level of model configuration through its desktop interface as Jan, we made most adjustments through Modelfiles and API requests. To keep our benchmarks comparable, we used the same settings as our previous tests: temperature 0.8, Top K 40, Top P 0.95, Min P 0.05, and a repeat penalty of 1.0. We also requested a batch size of 2,048, though we couldn’t independently verify whether Ollama applied it during generation.

GPU configuration was different as well, since there was no desktop setting equivalent to the 100 GPU layers we used in Jan. Ollama handled GPU offloading automatically, and a quick check using ollama ps confirmed that both imported models were running entirely on the RTX 5000 Ada.

We verified that report against NVIDIA’s own readings. Jan V3.5 increased VRAM allocation by several gigabytes after loading, and a live reading reached 93 percent GPU utilization during generation. Jan V2 also reported full GPU residency and showed 96 percent utilization in our diagnostic run. At least on this workstation, we didn’t have to work through a separate CUDA variant or GPU-layer setup to get accelerated generation.

For generation testing, we used the same prompt from our published Jan hands-on : “Explain RAID 5 and RAID 6 to someone building their first NAS. Include the main advantages and disadvantages of each, in about 400 words.” We disabled Web Search, set the context to 8,192 tokens, and included only that single user message in each API request. We discarded one warm-up response per model and then collected three measured runs.

Both models completed all three measured runs without generation failures, and GPU utilization stayed high throughout testing. Ollama required no additional CUDA configuration or manual GPU-layer adjustments to get both models running with full GPU acceleration, which was not the case in Open WebUI, where we added CUDA runtime DLLs by hand.

Note: Output-token counts, decode speeds, and GPU memory figures are medians of three measured runs after one discarded warm-up run. GPU memory is the median of the peak GPU-wide memory use recorded during each measured run.
*The Jan V3.5 GGUF filename identifies Q4_K_XL, while Ollama’s model information reports Q4_K_M; see the import notes above.

Jan V3.5 recorded 145.48, 145.73, and 145.44 tokens/sec across its measured runs, while Jan V2 recorded 92.87, 92.22, and 92.97 tokens/sec. Both sets stayed close from run to run, and the measured GPU memory peaks were unchanged within each set. Jan V2 produced considerably more reported output tokens, apparently including reasoning activity, so those totals are not a direct comparison of visible answer length.

On the same workstation and model files, those are the fastest results in this series so far. Jan V3.5 decoded 18 percent faster than in Jan itself (123 tokens/sec) and 26 percent faster than in Open WebUI Desktop (115.32), and Jan V2 was 13 percent ahead of Jan (82) and 24 percent ahead of Open WebUI (75.06). Each application runs its own llama.cpp build and manages GPU offload its own way, so the comparison reflects the complete package each one ships, not the model alone.

We did not publish prompt-processing medians because repeated requests produced very short timings that caching may have affected. Nor can runtime settings be identical in every respect: Jan exposed GPU layers directly, while Ollama managed offload automatically.

With the models installed, we selected Jan V3.5 or Jan V2 from the dropdown and entered the RAID prompt. Answers appeared with headings and lists, while recent conversations stayed in the sidebar. Ollama didn’t display generation rate or token count beneath responses, so we collected those figures via its API.
Jan V3.5 answers the RAID 5 versus RAID 6 prompt in Ollama’s desktop chat, with no token-rate display beneath the response.

Managing conversations in Ollama was easy enough, since right-clicking an earlier conversation brought up options to rename or delete it, with a Share option available under More tools. We could also go back and edit prompts we’d already sent, although there weren’t as many options for the model’s responses. The only button we found was Copy, which stays visible below each answer even when you’re not hovering over it. We couldn’t find a way to regenerate a response or view its generation statistics from the chat window, at least in the version we tested.

Ollama also has an Apps section with coding assistants, including Codex CLI, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Cline. We wanted to see how these integrations worked, so we clicked Codex CLI to see what setup involved. Ollama did not open a configuration screen; it copied a launch command to the clipboard and told us to paste it into a terminal. We didn’t complete the full installation or run Codex, but it gave us a better idea of how Ollama connects local models to external applications.
Selecting Codex CLI on the Apps page copied a launch command for the terminal; we didn’t run the integration itself.

Ollama places a globe button alongside the attachment control in Chat, but selecting it showed a message that Web Search requires an Ollama account. After signing up for a free account and enabling the feature, we used our existing test question asking for the latest stable Open WebUI release as of October 15, 2026, with a source citation.

We ran into another issue when testing Ollama’s Web Search feature: the application tried to retrieve results but returned a “search API error (status 402)” message instead. HTTP 402 is the Payment Required code, which suggests the search service needs a paid plan, though Ollama did not say so. The model suggested the problem might be related to account pricing or usage limits, but we couldn’t determine the exact cause. Since our local models were working normally, we decided not to spend more time troubleshooting the search service. It was still disappointing that we couldn’t complete the same Web Search test we’d attempted with the other applications in this series.
Ollama attempted our online version query but returned an HTTP 402 error from the search API.

Our first image test used the same Jan V2 VL High GGUF that worked with a separate vision projector in Jan. Ollama accepted the language-model file, but our import procedure did not associate the accompanying mmproj file. When we tried to attach the NVIDIA screenshot to a Jan V2 conversation, the desktop application displayed “This model does not support images” before we could send the prompt.
Our imported Jan V2 VL High model rejected the NVIDIA screenshot, reporting that it did not support images in this configuration.

We then tried Qwen3-VL 4B, downloaded through Ollama, using the same prompt asking for the GPU model, driver version, VRAM, utilization, temperature, and power. That model accepted the screenshot and finished with the correct six values: RTX 5000 Ada Generation, driver 597.06, 32,760 MiB, 0 percent utilization, 39C, and 40W. Its response was not perfect throughout, since it briefly gave an incorrect 8 percent utilization reading before correcting that value in the final summary.
Ollama’s Qwen3-VL 4B processed the attached NVIDIA screenshot and identified the hardware details; its final summary gave all six readings correctly.

In Ollama, we couldn’t paste an image directly from the Windows Snipping Tool into the chat window like we could with the other applications. Instead, we had to save the screenshot first, then upload it using the + button next to the message field. That worked without issues, and Ollama’s Qwen3-VL model analyzed the image successfully. Our imported Jan V2 model could not accept the same attachment, which limited our ability to repeat the original multimodal test.

Ollama’s local API was available as soon as its Windows service started, without launching a separate server from the desktop interface. A request to http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/models returned our installed Jan V3.5 and Qwen3-VL models, and a request to /v1/chat/completions using Jan V3.5 generated a one-sentence explanation of RAID 6.
The OpenAI-compatible local API returned Ollama’s installed model list and a RAID 6 chat response through PowerShell.

The response used slightly imprecise RAID 6 parity wording, which was a model-output issue, not an API failure. The working endpoint allowed us to query local models directly from PowerShell without using desktop chat.

The most frustrating issue we encountered was getting our imported Jan V2 VL High model to work with images. We had no problems importing the GGUF or running text prompts with full GPU acceleration, but things changed when we tried attaching our NVIDIA screenshot. Ollama told us the model didn’t support images because our import didn’t include the separate vision projector that Jan V2 requires. We could still complete the image-analysis test using Ollama’s Qwen3-VL download, which worked without issues. This showed that Ollama could process images, but getting our existing Jan V2 model to do the same wasn’t as simple as importing its GGUF file.

To use the Web Search feature, we had to create an Ollama account before we could enable it. Once we signed in and submitted our test question, the service returned an HTTP 402 error and no search results. We couldn’t determine what caused the error, and there wasn’t much reason to keep changing account settings or trying different plans without knowing whether that would help.

We also noticed how often we had to return to PowerShell for tasks like importing our existing models, adjusting their settings, and collecting performance measurements. The desktop application was easy to use for everyday chatting, but it didn’t offer the same level of control we had through Jan’s interface. Aside from these issues, Ollama gave us very little trouble during testing: both models imported successfully, all six measured benchmark runs completed, and the local API worked as expected.

Our testing with Ollama 0.40.11 generally went well, especially getting local models running on the RTX 5000 Ada. Both of our imported GGUFs worked with full GPU acceleration without requiring any additional CUDA setup, and performance led the series, with Jan V3.5 reaching a median of 145.48 tokens/sec and Jan V2 VL High reaching 92.87 tokens/sec, the fastest results in this series and 13 to 18 percent ahead of Jan on the same workstation. Once everything was configured, we had no problems moving between the desktop chat interface and the local API, and all measured benchmark runs completed without issues.

While we liked how simple Ollama was for everyday chatting, we would have preferred more control over individual models in the desktop application. Having to use PowerShell and create Modelfiles to import our existing GGUFs added a few extra steps, especially compared with Jan, where most of those settings are available directly in the interface. This won’t necessarily bother someone already familiar with running local models, but newcomers who want to manage everything through a graphical interface may find Ollama limiting. We also ran into a few issues with Web Search and our imported vision model, though neither affected normal text generation.

What we liked most about Ollama was how easily it could serve local models to other applications without requiring us to configure a separate server. The desktop chat is easy to get started with, while the local API and support for external coding tools let users do a lot more than chat with local models. We would still like to see better model-management controls in the desktop interface, but Ollama performed well on our workstation and gave us a dependable way to run both of our test models with GPU acceleration.
Leaderboard: Ollama holds Best Overall Local LLM Runtime on our Best Local LLM Tools page, where these results now sit beside our Jan and Open WebUI numbers.

We also requested a batch size of 2,048, though we couldn’t independently verify whether Ollama applied it during generation.

GPU configuration was different as well, since there was no desktop setting equivalent to the 100 GPU layers we used in Jan. Ollama handled GPU offloading automatically, and a quick check using ollama ps confirmed that both imported models were running entirely on the RTX 5000 Ada.

We verified that report against NVIDIA’s own readings. Jan V3.5 increased VRAM allocation by several gigabytes after loading, and a live reading reached 93 percent GPU utilization during generation. Jan V2 also reported full GPU residency and showed 96 percent utilization in our diagnostic run. At least on this workstation, we didn’t have to work through a separate CUDA variant or GPU-layer setup to get accelerated generation.

For generation testing, we used the same prompt from our published Jan hands-on : “Explain RAID 5 and RAID 6 to someone building their first NAS. Include the main advantages and disadvantages of each, in about 400 words.” We disabled Web Search, set the context to 8,192 tokens, and included only that single user message in each API request. We discarded one warm-up response per model and then collected three measured runs.

Both models completed all three measured runs without generation failures, and GPU utilization stayed high throughout testing. Ollama required no additional CUDA configuration or manual GPU-layer adjustments to get both models running with full GPU acceleration, which was not the case in Open WebUI, where we added CUDA runtime DLLs by hand.

Note: Output-token counts, decode speeds, and GPU memory figures are medians of three measured runs after one discarded warm-up run. GPU memory is the median of the peak GPU-wide memory use recorded during each measured run.
*The Jan V3.5 GGUF filename identifies Q4_K_XL, while Ollama’s model information reports Q4_K_M; see the import notes above.

Jan V3.5 recorded 145.48, 145.73, and 145.44 tokens/sec across its measured runs, while Jan V2 recorded 92.87, 92.22, and 92.97 tokens/sec. Both sets stayed close from run to run, and the measured GPU memory peaks were unchanged within each set. Jan V2 produced considerably more reported output tokens, apparently including reasoning activity, so those totals are not a direct comparison of visible answer length.

On the same workstation and model files, those are the fastest results in this series so far. Jan V3.5 decoded 18 percent faster than in Jan itself (123 tokens/sec) and 26 percent faster than in Open WebUI Desktop (115.32), and Jan V2 was 13 percent ahead of Jan (82) and 24 percent ahead of Open WebUI (75.06). Each application runs its own llama.cpp build and manages GPU offload its own way, so the comparison reflects the complete package each one ships, not the model alone.

We did not publish prompt-processing medians because repeated requests produced very short timings that caching may have affected. Nor can runtime settings be identical in every respect: Jan exposed GPU layers directly, while Ollama managed offload automatically.

With the models installed, we selected Jan V3.5 or Jan V2 from the dropdown and entered the RAID prompt. Answers appeared with headings and lists, while recent conversations stayed in the sidebar. Ollama didn’t display generation rate or token count beneath responses, so we collected those figures via its API.
Jan V3.5 answers the RAID 5 versus RAID 6 prompt in Ollama’s desktop chat, with no token-rate display beneath the response.

Managing conversations in Ollama was easy enough, since right-clicking an earlier conversation brought up options to rename or delete it, with a Share option available under More tools. We could also go back and edit prompts we’d already sent, although there weren’t as many options for the model’s responses. The only button we found was Copy, which stays visible below each answer even when you’re not hovering over it. We couldn’t find a way to regenerate a response or view its generation statistics from the chat window, at least in the version we tested.

Ollama also has an Apps section with coding assistants, including Codex CLI, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Cline. We wanted to see how these integrations worked, so we clicked Codex CLI to see what setup involved. Ollama did not open a configuration screen; it copied a launch command to the clipboard and told us to paste it into a terminal. We didn’t complete the full installation or run Codex, but it gave us a better idea of how Ollama connects local models to external applications.
Selecting Codex CLI on the Apps page copied a launch command for the terminal; we didn’t run the integration itself.

Ollama places a globe button alongside the attachment control in Chat, but selecting it showed a message that Web Search requires an Ollama account. After signing up for a free account and enabling the feature, we used our existing test question asking for the latest stable Open WebUI release as of October 15, 2026, with a source citation.

We ran into another issue when testing Ollama’s Web Search feature: the application tried to retrieve results but returned a “search API error (status 402)” message instead. HTTP 402 is the Payment Required code, which suggests the search service needs a paid plan, though Ollama did not say so. The model suggested the problem might be related to account pricing or usage limits, but we couldn’t determine the exact cause. Since our local models were working normally, we decided not to spend more time troubleshooting the search service. It was still disappointing that we couldn’t complete the same Web Search test we’d attempted with the other applications in this series.
Ollama attempted our online version query but returned an HTTP 402 error from the search API.

Our first image test used the same Jan V2 VL High GGUF that worked with a separate vision projector in Jan. Ollama accepted the language-model file, but our import procedure did not associate the accompanying mmproj file. When we tried to attach the NVIDIA screenshot to a Jan V2 conversation, the desktop application displayed “This model does not support images” before we could send the prompt.
Our imported Jan V2 VL High model rejected the NVIDIA screenshot, reporting that it did not support images in this configuration.

We then tried Qwen3-VL 4B, downloaded through Ollama, using the same prompt asking for the GPU model, driver version, VRAM, utilization, temperature, and power. That model accepted the screenshot and finished with the correct six values: RTX 5000 Ada Generation, driver 597.06, 32,760 MiB, 0 percent utilization, 39C, and 40W. Its response was not perfect throughout, since it briefly gave an incorrect 8 percent utilization reading before correcting that value in the final summary.
Ollama’s Qwen3-VL 4B processed the attached NVIDIA screenshot and identified the hardware details; its final summary gave all six readings correctly.

In Ollama, we couldn’t paste an image directly from the Windows Snipping Tool into the chat window like we could with the other applications. Instead, we had to save the screenshot first, then upload it using the + button next to the message field. That worked without issues, and Ollama’s Qwen3-VL model analyzed the image successfully. Our imported Jan V2 model could not accept the same attachment, which limited our ability to repeat the original multimodal test.

Ollama’s local API was available as soon as its Windows service started, without launching a separate server from the desktop interface. A request to http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/models returned our installed Jan V3.5 and Qwen3-VL models, and a request to /v1/chat/completions using Jan V3.5 generated a one-sentence explanation of RAID 6.
The OpenAI-compatible local API returned Ollama’s installed model list and a RAID 6 chat response through PowerShell.

The response used slightly imprecise RAID 6 parity wording, which was a model-output issue, not an API failure. The working endpoint allowed us to query local models directly from PowerShell without using desktop chat.

The most frustrating issue we encountered was getting our imported Jan V2 VL High model to work with images. We had no problems importing the GGUF or running text prompts with full GPU acceleration, but things changed when we tried attaching our NVIDIA screenshot. Ollama told us the model didn’t support images because our import didn’t include the separate vision projector that Jan V2 requires. We could still complete the image-analysis test using Ollama’s Qwen3-VL download, which worked without issues. This showed that Ollama could process images, but getting our existing Jan V2 model to do the same wasn’t as simple as importing its GGUF file.

To use the Web Search feature, we had to create an Ollama account before we could enable it. Once we signed in and submitted our test question, the service returned an HTTP 402 error and no search results. We couldn’t determine what caused the error, and there wasn’t much reason to keep changing account settings or trying different plans without knowing whether that would help.

We also noticed how often we had to return to PowerShell for tasks like importing our existing models, adjusting their settings, and collecting performance measurements. The desktop application was easy to use for everyday chatting, but it didn’t offer the same level of control we had through Jan’s interface. Aside from these issues, Ollama gave us very little trouble during testing: both models imported successfully, all six measured benchmark runs completed, and the local API worked as expected.

Our testing with Ollama 0.40.11 generally went well, especially getting local models running on the RTX 5000 Ada. Both of our imported GGUFs worked with full GPU acceleration without requiring any additional CUDA setup, and performance led the series, with Jan V3.5 reaching a median of 145.48 tokens/sec and Jan V2 VL High reaching 92.87 tokens/sec, the fastest results in this series and 13 to 18 percent ahead of Jan on the same workstation. Once everything was configured, we had no problems moving between the desktop chat interface and the local API, and all measured benchmark runs completed without issues.

While we liked how simple Ollama was for everyday chatting, we would have preferred more control over individual models in the desktop application. Having to use PowerShell and create Modelfiles to import our existing GGUFs added a few extra steps, especially compared with Jan, where most of those settings are available directly in the interface. This won’t necessarily bother someone already familiar with running local models, but newcomers who want to manage everything through a graphical interface may find Ollama limiting. We also ran into a few issues with Web Search and our imported vision model, though neither affected normal text generation.

What we liked most about Ollama was how easily it could serve local models to other applications without requiring us to configure a separate server. The desktop chat is easy to get started with, while the local API and support for external coding tools let users do a lot more than chat with local models. We would still like to see better model-management controls in the desktop interface, but Ollama performed well on our workstation and gave us a dependable way to run both of our test models with GPU acceleration.
Leaderboard: Ollama holds Best Overall Local LLM Runtime on our Best Local LLM Tools page, where these results now sit beside our Jan and Open WebUI numbers.

rssBodyEvidence: Vertiv announced SmartIT, a pre-engineered rack architecture that packages the rack, DC power conversion and distribution, direct-to-chip liquid cooling, in-rack coolant distribution, and monitoring into a factory-validated unit for NVIDIA MGX and OCP ORV3 systems. The supported list is NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, Vera Rubin NVL72, DGX Rubin NVL8, and HGX Rubin NVL8, and the product is available now worldwide. Vertiv’s enterprise configuration puts the envelope at 120 to 142kW per compute rack with 242kW of N+1 direct-to-chip cooling in the support rack beside it.

The solutions are aimed at enterprises, research institutions, and colocation providers that want NVL72-class systems in buildings that were not designed for them. Vertiv says SmartIT was previously deployed with NVIDIA to support the DGX GB300, scales from one rack to multi-rack deployments inside the same architecture, and arrives integrated and tested so on-site work is limited to facility power and water connections and commissioning. Site preparation, upstream power distribution, chilled or building water, and structural work stay outside the SmartIT scope.

The compute rack is the Vertiv Open Rack for NVIDIA MGX, with the NVL72 system itself supplied by NVIDIA. Vertiv lists it at 2,291.8mm tall including castors, 600mm wide, 1,068mm deep or 1,200mm with the extension, and 189kg empty. Power arrives as 50VDC from PowerDirect 33kW shelves over a DC busbar rated to 1,400A, and the in-rack manifolds carry coolant to the cold plates. The power shelves and CDU carry built-in monitoring with leak detection and an automated shunt-trip, and the platform speaks Redfish, SNMP, and Modbus northbound.

Enterprise deployments start with one compute rack and grow into one of two three-rack configurations. The support rack, SKU IRM692-362-VQE0M-N00 at 66kW, holds three CoolChip CDU 121 units at 121kW each, which is where the 242kW N+1 figure comes from, plus two PowerDirect shelves, the network switches, facility water loop isolation valves and actuators, an Avocent ACS 804 as the leak detection and response gateway, two Avocent RM1048P rack managers, and two PowerIT rack transfer switches. The storage rack, SKU IRM692-362-00E00-N00, swaps DC power for two 60A three-phase switched rPDUs with outlet-level monitoring at 69kVA total.

Each of the three racks gets a Liebert DCD47 rear door heat exchanger rated at 47kW room-neutral, so the configuration carries 141kW of supplemental air cooling on top of the liquid loop. A Liebert APM2 modular UPS with battery cabinet is optional, at up to 97.5 percent double-conversion efficiency. Installation, commissioning including flush and fill, and project management are included in the package, and Vertiv Global Services handles lifecycle support afterward.

The published numbers belong to the Blackwell configuration. Vertiv’s published enterprise configuration is built around a Blackwell-based NVL72 in the MGX rack, and the catalog lists two models, SmartIT for NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 and SmartIT for OCP ORV3, with identical rack dimensions. The Rubin systems appear on the supported list and in the HGX Rubin NVL8 demo unit Vertiv showed at NVIDIA GTC Berlin , but Vertiv has not published a power or cooling envelope for a Vera Rubin NVL72 build.

SmartIT is the rack-level piece of a stack Vertiv has been assembling around NVIDIA’s reference designs. Its CoolChip CDUs were among the first NVIDIA DSX Ready qualified components , its PowerDirect 33kW shelves are the 50VDC in-rack power stage it built for the GB300 NVL72 platform, with a GB200 NVL72 configuration also offered, and the company positions SmartRun for row-level integration and Unify for monitoring, analytics, and coordinated response across power and thermal gear once a site grows past a few racks.

“AI is fundamentally changing the demands placed on data center infrastructure, requiring closer coordination across power, cooling and IT systems to support increasingly complex workloads,” said Scott Armul, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Vertiv. “Vertiv SmartIT reflects our approach to solving that challenge by bringing these disciplines together in a factory-validated architecture. By combining Vertiv’s expertise across critical infrastructure, we’re helping customers simplify deployment, build greater consistency into their AI environments and establish a foundation that can evolve alongside their computing needs.”

rssBodyEvidence: Oracle announced a second round of Oracle Acceleron capabilities at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, a year after the networking suite first bundled dedicated fabrics, multiplanar networking, SmartNICs, and direct data paths for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The new pieces are RDMA on OCI’s shared front-end network, NVMe block storage attachments across Acceleron bare metal and VM shapes that Oracle rates at up to 3x the block performance, a collective communications plugin that moves failover and load balancing into the NCCL and RCCL layer, and multiplanar networking extended to front-end traffic.

“AI infrastructure can be unforgiving when it comes to network friction,” said Pradeep Vincent, executive vice president, Compute and AI Infrastructure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. “When thousands of accelerators are working together, one congested or failed path can have consequences far beyond a single connection. With Oracle Acceleron, we are building a network that can respond by rerouting traffic, recovering from failures, and helping customers scale securely.”

OCI’s front-end network carries Oracle Database, customer compute, block and object storage, SaaS and OCI services, backbone links, internet access, and on-premises connectivity on the same fabric, which is why RDMA has historically stayed on dedicated back-end cluster networks. The Oracle Acceleron High-Performance Fabric puts RDMA on that shared front end for inference, storage, and HPC traffic, and Oracle says it supports every queue pair type and verb, so existing RDMA applications run without changes. The company also uses the front-end links to connect separate GPU clusters while the back-end fabrics handle training inside each cluster.

The storage half is the expanded NVMe block storage attachment options across the new Acceleron bare metal and VM shapes, which Oracle says improve NVMe block storage performance by up to 3x for AI, database, and other data-intensive workloads. Oracle has not published the baseline configuration, the workload, or whether the figure is throughput, IOPS, or latency, and we did not run or audit it. The release carries Oracle’s standard future product disclaimer and gives no availability dates for any of the new capabilities.

Sharing a front end between RDMA and TCP is a congestion-control problem, since RDMA transports typically use rate-based control and TCP uses window-based control, and one loop can starve the other. Oracle’s answer lives in the Acceleron SmartNIC. Hierarchical token buckets track bandwidth for RDMA and non-RDMA classes under a shared parent bucket, and as tokens run low the NIC probabilistically marks ECN-capable packets or drops the rest, which produces a gradual congestion signal and also heads off incast at the top-of-rack link. Either class can borrow unused bandwidth from the other.

For congestion inside the fabric, the SmartNIC runs One-Way-Delay Congestion Control, measuring forward-path delay so that a congested reverse path does not trigger a false signal. When it sees elevated delay on a flow, it probes three alternate paths and moves the flow if one is better; if none is, it falls back to ECN marking or drops. Oracle describes the design as needing minimal QoS support from the switches while keeping standard kernel and CPU bypass on the hosts.

OCI’s back-end Multiplanar Network connects multi-port NICs to several disjoint fabrics so a training job has n-way redundancy, but using those planes has required NIC-level functionality that is not always available. The Oracle Collective Communications Library plugin removes that dependency. It is a CCL network plugin that natively supports the NVIDIA NCCL and AMD RCCL plugin interfaces, the layer frameworks use to turn collective operations into NIC transfers, and it carries failover, recovery, and congestion-aware load balancing inside the plugin, independent of NIC firmware and topology.

In operation, OCCL distributes collective traffic across multiple standard Reliable Connection queue pairs, sends more over the pairs showing higher throughput, and moves traffic off congested paths at the message and chunk level. When a port or a whole NIC fails, it steers the collective to another port or NIC so the job continues without a restart. Oracle’s framing is that this is simpler than routing controllers that pick fabric paths and watch for changes, and it works on single-plane and multi-plane networks alike. The same multiplanar path selection and failover now reaches front-end RDMA traffic through what Oracle calls Transparent Front-End Multiplanar Networking.

The same networking update covered two items outside Acceleron. OCI Global CDN Connect provides direct connections between OCI Object Storage and Cloudflare, Fastly, Netskrt, and Mainstreaming, with zero OCI egress charges on eligible cache fetches in supported regions, and Oracle has signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with F5 for a planned OCI App Defense web application and API protection service.

bodyEvidence: A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment . Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.
That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period .

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average new car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!)

That Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study , iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x , Lexus RZ300e , Honda Prologue , and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX , Kia EV6 , and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”
Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.

articles.title: First: Volvo CE Electric equipment does the work, without disturbing the wildlife
articles.summary: For the first time, electric equipment assets are being put to work in the National Wildlife Refuge System, where a battery-powered, zero-emission ECR25 Electric compact excavator and L25 Electric compact wheel loader made by Volvo CE are making the wild more accessible to everyone. more…
bodyEvidence: For the first time, electric equipment assets are being put to work in the National Wildlife Refuge System, where a battery-powered, zero-emission ECR25 Electric compact excavator and L25 Electric compact wheel loader made by Volvo CE are making the wild more accessible to everyone.

Construction work isn’t exactly welcome in the wilderness – between diesel exhaust, engine noises, and the constant rumble of heavy machinery, even a relatively small project can have a big impact on the native wildlife. To minimize that impact, US Fish and Wildlife Service is turning to Volvo CE and its compact excavators and wheel loaders to get the job done, building out a new, ADA accessible trail in Virginia’s Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge.

“We are excited to partner with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on this project to demonstrate Volvo’s commitment to lowering emissions and working to build the future we all want and need,” said Dr. Ray Gallant, VP of Product Management and Productivity, Volvo CE. “Projects like the one at the Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge give a glimpse of how electric machines can create a more climate-friendly future for the construction industry.”

The refuge is home to a diverse array of grasslands, wetlands, and woods that attract red foxes, painted turtles, osprey, river otters, and countless other rarely seen species – and the ADA accessible path being laid down by the L25 Electric compact wheel loader will allow wheelchair-bound visitors to travel a half-mile-long trail around one of the pond . Meanwhile, the ECR25 Electric compact excavator will be digging trenches to improve drainage from the pond and helping to place a viewing platform that extends out over the water.
Keeping the machines running is a portable EV ARC solar-powered charging system from Beam Global that’s designed to drive down the project’s carbon footprint even further.

rssBodyEvidence: General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.
articles.title: GM is recalling more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs over a brake software defect
articles.summary: General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking. more…
bodyEvidence: General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.
The recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.

After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.
When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.
In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.
In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:
According to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.
The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM said it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.
GM will update the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.

Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.
You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

articles.title: Ford Fathom EV pickup prices will range from $28,350 to the high $30Ks
articles.summary: Ford’s upcoming Fathom electric pickup will be among the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at $28,350. Even pricier trims will start at under $40,000. more…
bodyEvidence: Ford’s upcoming Fathom electric pickup will be among the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at $28,350. Even pricier trims will start at under $40,000.
After announcing the name of its new midsize electric pickup this summer, Ford said the Fathom will start at just $28,350 for the standard-range model.

Even with the $1,595 delivery fee, prices will start at under $30,000. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Jim Farley said the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle off the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.
Last Tuesday, a day before earnings, Farley said he had the chance to test-drive a prototype and that it “completely blew me away.”
The 0 to 60 mph, huge room inside, and the hands-free, ADAS experience was like “something I’ve never experienced,” Farley told investors.
Ford’s CEO added that the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and affordable. The MSRP under $30,000 and low cost of ownership, Farley said, is perfect for today’s market.

The electric pickup will use a zonal electrical architecture and a 48-volt system to cut costs. It will also offer bidirectional charging, enabling it to power your home to save on energy costs or during an outage.
When asked how the company plans to upsell the Fathom beyond the $28,350 starting price, Andrew Frick, president of Ford Model e, offered some insight.
“The starting price of $28,350 is just that,” Frick said. “We’ll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range. And we’ll have a couple of different offerings within that,” he explained.
Frick said it’s too soon to share more about the offerings themselves at this point, and more details will come closer to launch.
According to Farley, the embedded Apple Maps is a “game changer” for any EV, but especially for a vehicle starting under $30,000.
“That is going to be the most exciting upsell opportunity,” Farley said, “it’s really the long-term subscription and digital experience for the customer.”
Apple Maps will be directly integrated into the navigation system. All Fathom models will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.
We still haven’t seen the interior, but Ford claims the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.

I almost feel like the Fathom will be utilized similarly to how the Maverick is utilized and possibly become a big seller as well. It seems well suited for a small business work vehicle as well with fuel savings by going electric to add to the appeal.

The midsize electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and that’s not including the frunk (front trunk) or truck bed. Ford also said the Fathom will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.
We also know the Fathom will have an NACS port after a prototype was caught at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.
Ford is set to open preorders in early 2027, with an official launch expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

articles.title: Range Rover is axing its two cheapest SUVs, making way for a new entry-level EV
articles.summary: Range Rover is pulling the plug on its two most affordable models, the Evoque and Velar, as a new entry-level EV steps in. more…
bodyEvidence: Range Rover is pulling the plug on its two most affordable models, the Evoque and Velar, as a new entry-level EV steps in.
For decades, the Range Rover name was viewed as a status symbol, mostly used by wealthy buyers, high-powered executives, and even royalty.
That started to change with the launch of the Evoque in 2011 and the Velar in 2017, making the iconic British luxury brand a little more accessible.

In the US, the 2026 Range Rover Evoque starts at $49,900, and the Velar starts at $61,600. That’s considerably less than the Sport and flagship Range Rover SUVs, which start at $83,700 and $107,400, respectively.

Range Rover’s accessible luxury era is reportedly drawing to a close. Martin Limbert, Range Rover’s managing director, confirmed to Autocar that the Evoque and Velar will officially be discontinued, with production set to end in 2027.
While it has no direct replacement planned, the new Range Rover GT will serve as the brand’s new entry-level vehicle.
Range Rover revealed the GT in July, presenting it as the fifth and newest member of the lineup. Unlike the distinct SUV design Range Rover has built the brand on, the GT is a low-slung grand tourer.
The electric GT is “a captivating new expression” of the brand, Range said, describing it as “the most technologically sophisticated” model it’s ever designed.

It’s expected to be among the first vehicles based on JLR’s new EMA platform. Initially, the Range Rover GT will launch as a battery-electric vehicle (BEV), but Range Rover plans to add a full-hybrid (HEV) option later in the lifecycle.
Production of the Range Rover GT is set to begin in the first half of 2027 at JLR’s Halewood, UK plant, following the flagship electric SUV and smaller Sport EV model (shown below).
The Range Rover GT is expected to start at around $90,000 with an EPA range of at least 300 miles when it goes on sale as a 2028 model. In the UK, it will likely be over £75,000 ($100,000).
Range Rover’s flagship electric SUV starts at $140,450 in the US, and the smaller Sport EV will likely be a bit cheaper at around $120,000 to $130,000.
At $90,000, the electric GT isn’t what most would consider an “entry-level” vehicle, but it’s part of Range Rover’s push into higher-end, more profitable models.
